domain_name: Internal control frameworks and SOX scope

questions.subtopic: 5A1 The original framework (1992). Definition of internal control
questions.question: A controller tells the new finance team that a well-run system of internal control, as COSO first defined it in 1992, guarantees the company will meet its objectives. Which correction is MOST accurate?

options.A: It gives reasonable assurance, limited to financial reporting objectives
options.B: It gives assurance once the independent auditor has tested it
options.C: It gives reasonable, not absolute, assurance on its objectives
options.D: It gives absolute assurance once the five components are in place

questions.key_concept: COSO internal control gives reasonable, not absolute, assurance across operations, reporting and compliance objectives.
questions.pre_read: Recall COSO's core definition: who carries out internal control, what level of assurance it gives, and over which objectives.
questions.correct_explanation: COSO defines internal control as a process carried out by the board, management and other personnel that gives reasonable assurance about achieving objectives. Assurance stays reasonable, not absolute, because judgment can be faulty, people make errors, and management can override controls or staff can collude. The definition spans operations, reporting and compliance objectives; financial reporting alone is the SEC's narrower ICFR slice.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: reasonable assurance is right, but COSO's definition also covers operations and compliance objectives. Financial reporting alone is the SEC's narrower ICFR definition.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because audits add confidence. But the board, management and staff carry out internal control; an auditor's test is not what creates the assurance.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because five components sound complete. But COSO says even an effective system gives only reasonable assurance; override, collusion and simple error remain possible.

tips: Eliminate: D promises absolute assurance and B ties assurance to the auditor; COSO limits internal control to reasonable assurance, carried out by the company's own people.
Final two: C beats A because COSO's definition spans operations, reporting and compliance; financial reporting alone is the SEC's narrower ICFR definition.
Exam cue: an option promising certainty or a guarantee from internal control is wrong; COSO always says reasonable assurance.

questions.subtopic: 5A1 The original framework (1992). Cube faces
questions.question: A compliance team is labeling the faces of COSO's original 1992 internal control cube for a training slide. Which list BEST names the framework's objective categories?

options.A: Operations, financial reporting and compliance
options.B: Strategic, operations, reporting and compliance
options.C: Control environment, control activities and monitoring
options.D: Entity level, divisions and operating units

questions.key_concept: The 1992 COSO framework has three objective categories: operations, financial reporting and compliance.
questions.pre_read: The cube has three faces. Ask which face holds what the entity aims for, as opposed to what it needs or where it acts.
questions.correct_explanation: The 1992 framework set three objective categories: effective and efficient operations, reliable financial reporting, and compliance with applicable laws and regulations, as the SEC's Release No. 33-8238 records. The five components form a second face of the cube and the entity's units the third. A strategic category arrived later, in COSO's 2004 ERM framework, not in the internal control framework.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: these are the four objective categories of COSO's 2004 ERM framework. The internal control framework has no strategic category.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because these sit on the cube too. But they are components, which form a different face from the objectives.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the cube has an organizational face. But entity level, divisions and units are its third dimension, not objectives.

tips: Eliminate: C lists components and D lists the entity's structure; both are other faces of the cube, not objectives.
Final two: A beats B because the strategic category belongs to the 2004 ERM framework; internal control has three objective categories.
Exam cue: four categories including strategic point to ERM; three without it point to the internal control framework.

questions.subtopic: 5A2 The 2013 update. Framework choice
questions.question: The CFO of an issuer in its third year of SEC reporting asks whether SEC rules require the COSO framework for management's annual ICFR evaluation. What is the MOST accurate answer?

options.A: No; the independent auditor selects the framework instead
options.B: Yes; the SEC's rules name COSO as the mandatory framework
options.C: No; management may use any checklist it designs itself
options.D: No; any suitable framework set through due process qualifies

questions.key_concept: Management must use a suitable, recognized framework set through due process; COSO qualifies but is not mandated.
questions.pre_read: Look for the test the rule sets for a framework, and whether the SEC named one framework as compulsory.
questions.correct_explanation: Rule 13a-15(c) requires management to base its evaluation on a suitable, recognized control framework set by a body that followed due process, including broad distribution for public comment. In Release No. 33-8238 the SEC said COSO satisfies its criteria but chose not to mandate any framework, since others exist or may be developed. Item 308(a)(2) then requires management's report to name the framework used.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the auditor attests under 404(b). But Rule 13a-15(c) puts the evaluation, and so the framework choice, on management.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: the SEC accepted COSO as meeting its criteria, but Release No. 33-8238 expressly declines to mandate COSO or any single framework.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the SEC allows flexibility. But Rule 13a-15(c) requires a recognized framework from a due-process body, not an in-house checklist.

tips: Eliminate: C fails the due-process test for a framework, and A gives management's evaluation to the auditor; Rule 13a-15(c) puts both on management.
Final two: D beats B because the SEC said COSO satisfies its criteria yet chose not to mandate it; any suitable, recognized framework works.
Exam cue: suitable, recognized and set through due process is the test; COSO passes it but is not compulsory.

questions.subtopic: 5A2 The 2013 update. Structure after the update
questions.question: A compliance analyst on the SOX team is updating training written for the 1992 COSO framework. Which statement BEST describes what the 2013 update did to the framework's structure?

options.A: Added a sixth component for information technology controls
options.B: Kept the five components and set out 17 principles under them
options.C: Kept the five components and listed principles as optional guidance
options.D: Replaced the five components with eight risk components

questions.key_concept: COSO 2013 kept the five components and set out 17 principles that relevant controls must satisfy.
questions.pre_read: Separate what the update kept from what it added, and ask whether the additions are requirements or aids.
questions.correct_explanation: The 2013 update kept the 1992 definition of internal control and its five components, then set out 17 principles drawn from those components. Effective internal control needs each component and each relevant principle to be present and functioning, so the principles are requirements, not options. COSO presumes all 17 are relevant and accepts exceptions only in rare industry, operating or regulatory situations.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because technology gained weight in 2013. But it appears as principle 11 under control activities; there are still five components.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: the components were kept, but COSO presumes every principle is relevant and requires relevant principles to be present and functioning. Points of focus are the optional aids.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because COSO's 2004 ERM framework has eight components. But the internal control framework kept its five; eight belongs to ERM.

tips: Eliminate: A and D change the number of components; the 2013 update kept exactly five, made technology a principle and left eight components to ERM.
Final two: B beats C because relevant principles must be present and functioning; only the points of focus are optional aids.
Exam cue: COSO 2013 in one line: same definition, same five components, 17 principles that count.

questions.subtopic: 5A2 The 2013 update. Rating a deficiency
questions.question: A U.S. issuer's SOX team uses COSO 2013 for its Section 404 assessment and must rate a control deficiency's severity. Which approach does COSO's own guidance MOST directly support?

options.A: Last year's severity rating carried forward for consistency
options.B: A pass or fail score for each point of focus
options.C: The SEC's terms: significant deficiency and material weakness
options.D: COSO's own 'major deficiency' test, used in place of SEC terms

questions.key_concept: SEC filers rate deficiency severity only with the SEC's definitions, as COSO's 2013 guidance directs.
questions.pre_read: Ask whose definitions govern severity when a regulator has set its own criteria for the report.
questions.correct_explanation: COSO's 2013 FAQ says that where laws, rules or regulators set criteria for classifying deficiencies, management uses only those criteria rather than the framework's own classifications. A company reporting to the SEC therefore rates severity as a control deficiency, significant deficiency or material weakness. Under COSO's FAQ, a material weakness as the SEC defines it means ICFR does not meet the framework's requirements, and Item 308(a)(3) bars an effective conclusion.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because consistency feels efficient. But each deficiency's severity is judged on its own facts under the SEC's definitions, not inherited from a prior rating.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because points of focus support assessment. But COSO does not require them to be assessed separately, and they are not a severity scale.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: COSO uses 'major deficiency' in its own effectiveness test, but it tells entities reporting under SEC rules to use the SEC's definitions instead.

tips: Eliminate: B treats points of focus as a severity scale and A inherits last year's rating; neither applies the SEC's definitions to this deficiency.
Final two: C beats D because COSO tells SEC filers to classify severity only with the SEC's definitions, not the framework's own term.
Exam cue: when COSO meets SOX, the SEC's words decide severity: control deficiency, significant deficiency, material weakness.

questions.subtopic: 5A2 The 2013 update. Framework statement
questions.question: A controller reviewing a 2026 Form 10-K draft sees that management's ICFR report concludes ICFR is effective but never names its framework, which was COSO 2013. Under Item 308(a), what is the fix?

options.A: Identify COSO's 2013 framework as the one management used
options.B: Name the 1992 edition, still COSO's current one
options.C: Keep it, since a conclusion alone meets the rule
options.D: Leave it out; the auditor's report names the framework

questions.key_concept: Item 308(a)(2) requires management's ICFR report to identify the framework used to evaluate ICFR.
questions.pre_read: Check what Item 308(a) says management's own report must state, beyond the conclusion on effectiveness.
questions.correct_explanation: Item 308(a)(2) requires management's annual ICFR report to include a statement identifying the framework management used to evaluate effectiveness, so a conclusion alone does not meet the rule. Management used COSO's 2013 framework, so the report should say so. Naming the edition goes beyond the rule's text but follows COSO's request that external reports state which edition was applied; COSO treats the 1992 edition as superseded after 15 December 2014.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because many companies began with it. But management used the 2013 framework, and COSO considered the 1992 edition superseded after 15 December 2014.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: the conclusion is required too, under Item 308(a)(3), but Item 308(a)(2) separately requires a statement identifying the framework management used.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the auditor also reports on ICFR. But Item 308(a)(2) puts the framework statement in management's own report.

tips: Eliminate: B names a superseded edition management did not use, and D drops a statement Item 308(a)(2) requires in management's own report.
Final two: A beats C because Item 308(a)(2) requires a statement identifying the framework management used.
Exam cue: management's ICFR report states responsibility, framework, conclusion and any material weakness; vague framework wording gets fixed, not removed.

questions.subtopic: 5A2 The 2013 update. Placing an activity
questions.question: During annual planning, a retailer's finance team studies how bonus pressure could push store managers to inflate quarterly sales. Under COSO 2013, where does this activity MOST directly belong?

options.A: Control environment, under the principle on accountability
options.B: Monitoring activities, under the principle on separate evaluations
options.C: Control activities, under the principle on technology controls
options.D: Risk assessment, under the principle on considering fraud

questions.key_concept: Considering how pressure or incentives could lead to fraud is risk assessment principle 8 in COSO 2013.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether the team is setting incentives, testing existing controls, or analyzing what could go wrong.
questions.correct_explanation: Principle 8, in the risk assessment component, covers fraud risk: the team is weighing how incentives could lead to fraudulent reporting. The control environment covers performance measures, incentives and accountability, which makes it tempting, and pressure on staff matters there too. But its accountability principle is about holding people responsible for their internal control duties; analyzing how pressure could produce fraud belongs to risk assessment.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: incentives, pressure and accountability are control environment matters, but accountability means holding people responsible; analyzing how pressure could cause fraudulent reporting is principle 8 under risk assessment.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the study happens yearly. But separate evaluations check whether controls are present and functioning; they do not assess fraud risk.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because sales data lives in systems. But principle 11 covers general controls over technology, not the analysis of fraud risk.

tips: Eliminate: C covers technology controls and B covers testing existing controls; neither is the analysis of fraud risk the team is doing.
Final two: D beats A because Principle 5's "considers excessive pressures" is about accountability; analyzing how pressure could lead to fraud is Principle 8, in risk assessment.
Exam cue: considering the potential for fraud is risk assessment; integrity, oversight, structure, competence and accountability are control environment.

questions.subtopic: 5A2 The 2013 update. Effectiveness test
questions.question: A distributor's approved policy sets up an ethics hotline, but management's year-end review finds no call was answered all year. Under COSO 2013, which conclusion about the related principle is MOST accurate?

options.A: Present and functioning, because the policy is approved and published
options.B: Designed but not operating; assess the deficiency's severity
options.C: Not relevant, because management may drop any principle it chooses
options.D: Acceptable, because COSO assesses components rather than principles

questions.key_concept: A principle in design but not operating has a deficiency; management judges its severity to conclude whether the principle is present and functioning.
questions.pre_read: Separate what the policy shows from what actually happened during the year, then ask what COSO 2013 tests.
questions.correct_explanation: COSO 2013 requires each component and relevant principle to be present and functioning, with the components operating together. The approved policy shows the hotline exists in design, but unanswered calls all year show it did not operate. COSO's FAQ has management judge that deficiency's severity; if it is a major deficiency, the principle, and so its component, is not present and functioning.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the policy exists. But an approved policy shows presence at most; functioning needs evidence the hotline actually operated.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because COSO allows judgment. But it presumes all 17 principles are relevant and accepts exceptions only in rare situations.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: the 1992 edition was read at component level, but COSO 2013 tests relevant principles too, so a deficiency in one must be judged for severity.

tips: Eliminate: A counts paper as performance and C treats principles as optional; COSO needs evidence of operation and presumes every principle is relevant.
Final two: B beats D because COSO 2013 tests relevant principles: a hotline that never operated is a deficiency whose severity management must judge, not something waved through at component level.
Exam cue: policy on paper shows design; evidence it worked shows operation. A gap is a deficiency to judge, and a major one means the principle is not present and functioning.

questions.subtopic: 5B1 ERM (2004) and how it differs from internal control. Components compared
questions.question: A risk manager is comparing COSO's 2004 ERM framework with the internal control framework for the risk committee. Which component BEST shows what the 2004 ERM framework added?

options.A: Risk assessment
options.B: Event identification
options.C: Governance and culture
options.D: Information and communication

questions.key_concept: COSO ERM 2004 added objective setting, event identification and risk response to internal control's components.
questions.pre_read: List the eight 2004 ERM components, then strike out the ones internal control already has.
questions.correct_explanation: COSO's 2004 ERM framework has eight components: internal environment, objective setting, event identification, risk assessment, risk response, control activities, information and communication, and monitoring. Event identification, like objective setting and risk response, has no counterpart among internal control's five components. Governance and culture is a component of the 2017 ERM update, not of the 2004 framework.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because ERM is about risk. But risk assessment is also one of internal control's five components, so ERM did not add it.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: governance and culture is an ERM component, but of the 2017 update. The 2004 framework opens with the internal environment instead.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it is on the ERM list. But information and communication is also an internal control component, so ERM did not add it.

tips: Eliminate: A and D appear in both frameworks, so neither shows what the 2004 ERM framework added.
Final two: B beats C because governance and culture belongs to ERM 2017; event identification is a 2004 addition with no internal control counterpart.
Exam cue: ERM 2004's extras are objective setting, event identification and risk response; governance and culture signals ERM 2017.

questions.subtopic: 5B1 ERM (2004) and how it differs from internal control. ERM and Section 404
questions.question: A director at a large accelerated filer argues that, since the company adopted COSO's 2004 ERM framework, its Section 404 work can now follow ERM alone. What is the CFO's BEST response?

options.A: ERM is narrower and fits inside the internal control framework
options.B: ERM replaced the internal control framework for Section 404 purposes
options.C: Section 404 requires large accelerated filers to adopt ERM
options.D: ERM is broader; Section 404 still needs an assessment of ICFR

questions.key_concept: ERM is broader than internal control but does not replace the Section 404 assessment of ICFR.
questions.pre_read: Recall how COSO describes the relationship between ERM and internal control, then what Section 404 asks management to assess.
questions.correct_explanation: COSO describes enterprise risk management as broader than internal control, with internal control an integral part of it, and calls the two frameworks complementary, with neither superseding the other. Section 404(a) and Item 308(a) require management to assess internal control over financial reporting against a suitable framework. Adopting ERM supports strategy and enterprise risk, but it does not replace the ICFR assessment.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the two share components. But COSO says ERM is broader than internal control and includes it, not the reverse.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: ERM does include internal control, but COSO says neither framework supersedes the other, and Section 404 asks specifically for an assessment of ICFR.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because large accelerated filers face more rules. But COSO notes entities may not be required to apply ERM; Section 404 requires reporting on ICFR.

tips: Eliminate: A reverses the relationship, since ERM is the broader framework, and C invents an ERM duty that no SOX provision imposes.
Final two: D beats B because the frameworks are complementary and neither supersedes the other, while Section 404 asks for an assessment of ICFR.
Exam cue: ERM contains internal control but does not replace it; Section 404 tests internal control over financial reporting.

questions.subtopic: 5B1 ERM (2004) and how it differs from internal control. Status after 2013
questions.question: A risk analyst's memo to the risk committee says COSO's 2013 internal control update superseded the 2004 ERM framework on 15 December 2014. Which correction BEST fits COSO's own statements?

options.A: The memo is right; the 2013 update absorbed ERM into its principles
options.B: ERM became a sixth internal control component on that date
options.C: That date retired the 1992 internal control edition, not ERM
options.D: ERM was retired on that date by COSO's 2017 ERM update

questions.key_concept: 15 December 2014 ended the 1992 internal control edition; COSO says internal control and ERM are complementary.
questions.pre_read: Ask which COSO publication the 15 December 2014 date belongs to, and how COSO describes the two frameworks' relationship.
questions.correct_explanation: COSO set 15 December 2014 as the end of the transition for its 1992 internal control framework, after which it treated that edition as superseded. The 2013 update did not change the relationship with ERM: COSO calls the two frameworks complementary, says neither supersedes the other, and kept the ERM framework as suitable for enterprise risk management. ERM was updated separately in 2017.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: ERM does contain internal control, but COSO said the 2013 update was not meant to alter that relationship and neither framework supersedes the other.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because ERM overlaps with internal control. But the 2013 framework kept exactly five components; ERM stayed a separate framework.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because ERM was later updated. But that update came in 2017, years after the date that retired the 1992 internal control edition.

tips: Eliminate: B adds a component the 2013 framework never had, and D puts a 2017 publication on a 2014 date.
Final two: C beats A because COSO says the two frameworks are complementary and neither supersedes the other; the 2014 date ended the 1992 edition.
Exam cue: 15 December 2014 belongs to the 1992 internal control framework; ERM's own update came in 2017.

questions.subtopic: 5B2 ERM (2017): strategy and performance. Structure of the update
questions.question: A risk officer preparing a board briefing on COSO's 2017 ERM update must describe its structure. Which description is MOST accurate?

options.A: Five components supported by 20 principles
options.B: Four objective categories with no components
options.C: Five components supported by 17 principles
options.D: Eight components arranged in a three-dimensional cube

questions.key_concept: COSO ERM 2017 is 20 principles organized into five components.
questions.pre_read: Keep three COSO counts apart: internal control 2013, ERM 2004 and ERM 2017.
questions.correct_explanation: COSO's 2017 update, Enterprise Risk Management—Integrating with Strategy and Performance, is a set of 20 principles organized into five components: governance and culture; strategy and objective-setting; performance; review and revision; and information, communication and reporting. Seventeen principles belong to the 2013 internal control framework, while eight components and a cube describe the 2004 ERM framework.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because ERM 2004 used four objective categories. But the 2017 update is organized as components and principles, so 'no components' is wrong.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: five components is right, but 17 is the principle count of the 2013 internal control framework. ERM 2017 has 20 principles.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it describes COSO ERM. But eight components and the cube are the 2004 edition, which the 2017 update reorganized.

tips: Eliminate: D describes the 2004 edition and B leaves out the components the 2017 update is built on.
Final two: A beats C because 17 principles belong to the 2013 internal control framework; ERM 2017 has 20.
Exam cue: internal control 2013 has 5 and 17, ERM 2004 has 8 components, ERM 2017 has 5 and 20.

questions.subtopic: 5B2 ERM (2017): strategy and performance. Choosing a strategy
questions.question: A board is choosing between two growth strategies, and management presents only the risks that could derail the strategy it already prefers. Under COSO's 2017 ERM framework, what is the MOST important gap?

options.A: No Section 404 test of the preferred strategy's controls
options.B: No complete inventory of every risk across the enterprise
options.C: No view of each strategy's fit with the mission and risk profile
options.D: No internal audit sign-off approving the preferred strategy

questions.key_concept: ERM 2017 weighs each strategy's fit with the mission and its risk profile, not only risks to the chosen strategy.
questions.pre_read: COSO 2017 names three aspects of risk in strategy. Count how many the presentation covers.
questions.correct_explanation: COSO's 2017 framework says risk to the chosen strategy is only one aspect. Two others can affect value more: the possibility that a strategy does not align with the mission, vision and core values, and the implications, meaning the risk profile, of each alternative. Presenting only risks to the preferred option skips both, so the board cannot weigh the alternatives against its risk appetite.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because SOX testing is familiar. But Section 404 covers internal control over financial reporting, not the choice of business strategy.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: an inventory feels thorough, but COSO says ERM is more than a risk listing; the gap here is the comparison of strategies.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because assurance sounds prudent. But COSO puts strategy review with the board and management; internal audit does not approve strategy.

tips: Eliminate: D gives strategy approval to internal audit and A stretches Section 404 to business strategy; neither is what ERM 2017 asks for.
Final two: C beats B because COSO 2017 says ERM is more than a risk list; the missing pieces are mission fit and each alternative's risk profile.
Exam cue: ERM 2017 asks three things of a strategy: risks to it, fit with the mission, and the risk profile it brings.

questions.subtopic: 5C1 Software and spreadsheets. General controls evaluated
questions.question: Under SEC Release No. 33-8810, which IT general controls must management evaluate in its ICFR assessment?

options.A: Every control in development, changes, operations and access
options.B: Those that other key controls depend on to operate consistently
options.C: None, because the independent auditor alone tests general controls
options.D: Only those over systems the independent auditor plans to rely on

questions.key_concept: Management evaluates only the IT general controls needed for in-scope controls to operate properly and consistently.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the general controls are for in an ICFR assessment, and whether the SEC's list of areas is a checklist.
questions.correct_explanation: Release No. 33-8810 says management only needs to evaluate the IT general controls necessary for the proper and consistent operation of other controls that address financial reporting risks. It names program development, program changes, computer operations and access to programs and data as example areas, not a mandatory checklist, and says general controls that mainly serve operational efficiency need not be evaluated.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: those are the SEC's example areas, but the guidance says they may not all apply; management evaluates only the general controls that in-scope controls rely on.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because auditors test IT. But management must evaluate ICFR itself under Rule 13a-15(c), including the general controls its key controls depend on.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because auditors scope IT around reliance. But management's evaluation is its own: it covers the general controls its key controls depend on, whatever the auditor plans.

tips: Eliminate: C hands management's evaluation to the auditor, and D ties it to the auditor's plans; management scopes its own evaluation from its key controls.
Final two: B beats A because the SEC's four areas are examples; only the general controls that in-scope controls depend on need evaluating.
Exam cue: under the SEC's guidance, general controls matter as far as key controls lean on them, and no further.

questions.subtopic: 5C1 Software and spreadsheets. Spreadsheet scope
questions.question: A manufacturer's tax team computes the year-end income tax provision in a spreadsheet and posts the result to the general ledger. For Section 404, how should management BEST treat the spreadsheet?

options.A: Out of scope until IT registers it as a system of record
options.B: Out of scope once the independent auditor recalculates the provision
options.C: Covered by the ledger's general controls, so no separate controls
options.D: In scope, with controls over its access, formulas and changes

questions.key_concept: A spreadsheet is in SOX scope when a key financial reporting calculation depends on it, however IT classifies it.
questions.pre_read: Follow the provision from calculation to ledger and ask where the financial reporting risk sits.
questions.correct_explanation: Scope follows financial reporting risk, not the type of tool. The tax provision is calculated in the spreadsheet, so the control over it depends on the spreadsheet's formulas working consistently, which Release No. 33-8810 (Section II.A.1.d, footnote 35) gives as IT functionality a control depends on. Management therefore brings the spreadsheet into scope with controls over access, formula changes and inputs, and keeps evidence for its assessment.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: system-of-record labels help IT inventories, but SOX scope follows the financial reporting risk; a calculation feeding the ledger is in scope however it is labeled.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the auditor checks the provision. But the auditor's work is not management's control, and management must evaluate its own ICFR.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the ledger has strong IT controls. But they protect the ledger, not the spreadsheet formulas that produce the provision posted to it.

tips: Eliminate: C relies on ledger controls that never touch the spreadsheet's formulas, and B treats the auditor's work as management's control.
Final two: D beats A because scope follows the financial reporting risk, not whether IT has labeled the tool a system of record.
Exam cue: if a material number is calculated in a tool, that tool is in scope, spreadsheet or not.

questions.subtopic: 5C1 Software and spreadsheets. Packaged software
questions.question: A retailer's revenue runs through a packaged, off-the-shelf billing application whose automated pricing controls address a key revenue risk. For its Section 404 evaluation, which approach is BEST for management?

options.A: Evaluate the automated controls and the general controls behind them
options.B: Exclude the application, since purchased software is outside SOX scope
options.C: Evaluate the general controls alone, since they cover automated logic
options.D: Exclude the application if the vendor certifies it each year

questions.key_concept: Automated controls in purchased software are in scope, evaluated together with the IT general controls they rely on.
questions.pre_read: Ask what actually addresses the revenue risk here, and what keeps it working.
questions.correct_explanation: When a control that addresses a financial reporting risk is automated, Release No. 33-8810 says management's evaluation considers the automated application controls and the relevant IT general controls over the application. General controls alone ordinarily do not address financial reporting risks; they support the consistent operation of the automated controls. Buying the software rather than building it does not change its scope.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because a vendor built it. But scope follows the risk the controls address, not whether the software was bought or built.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: general controls matter, but the SEC says they alone ordinarily do not address financial reporting risks; the automated pricing controls must be evaluated too.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because certification sounds like assurance. But a vendor's general statement does not test this retailer's controls, and management must still evaluate its own ICFR.

tips: Eliminate: B and D take the application out of scope, yet its automated controls address a key revenue risk, so it stays in.
Final two: A beats C because the SEC says general controls alone ordinarily do not address financial reporting risks; the automated controls need evaluating too.
Exam cue: automated control in scope means test it plus the general controls it leans on, whoever wrote the code.

questions.subtopic: 5C1 Software and spreadsheets. Spreadsheet change
questions.question: Management lets only authorized analysts open a revenue-allocation spreadsheet used for the annual report, but their formula edits are neither logged nor approved, and reviewers check totals. Which control area is MOST weakened?

options.A: Logical access to the spreadsheet file
options.B: Program development for new spreadsheet models
options.C: Change control over the spreadsheet's formulas
options.D: Computer operations, such as backups and job scheduling

questions.key_concept: Unlogged, unapproved formula edits are a change-control failure, even when access is properly limited.
questions.pre_read: The stem settles one control area for you. Find it, then ask what users can still do unchecked.
questions.correct_explanation: The stem says access is already limited to authorized analysts, so the weakness is what those users can do unchecked: change formulas with no log or approval. That is the program-change area of IT general controls applied to a spreadsheet, which needs approved, recorded changes and a kept version. A review of totals cannot reliably catch a broken formula, so change control is the gap that most threatens the allocation.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: access matters for spreadsheets, but the stem says only authorized analysts can open the file. Unlogged, unapproved formula edits are a change-control failure.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it is one of the SEC's four example areas. But program development covers building new tools; editing an existing formula is a program change.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because backups protect files. But computer operations covers running and recovering systems, not approving formula changes.

tips: Eliminate: D covers running and recovering systems and B covers building new models; neither addresses unapproved edits to an existing formula.
Final two: C beats A because the stem already limits access to authorized analysts; what is missing is approval and logging of their changes.
Exam cue: right people, wrong edits points to change control; wrong people points to access.

questions.subtopic: 5C2 Service organizations: from SAS 70 to SSAE 18. Responsibility
questions.question: A bank outsources loan servicing to a service organization whose processing feeds the bank's financial statements. Who has the PRIMARY responsibility for assessing controls over that process for Section 404?

options.A: The bank's management, using evidence such as a Type 2 report
options.B: The service auditor, by issuing its report on the provider
options.C: The bank's independent auditor, as part of its 404(b) attestation
options.D: The service organization's management, which runs those controls

questions.key_concept: User-company management keeps Section 404 responsibility for outsourced processes and may rely on a Type 2 report.
questions.pre_read: Separate who performs the processing, who reports on it, and whose annual ICFR assessment covers it.
questions.correct_explanation: The SEC staff's ICFR FAQ says that when management outsources functions, it keeps the responsibility to assess controls over the outsourced operations. Management may rely on a service auditor's Type 2 report as evidence and remains responsible for controls over information flowing to and from the provider. Under Section 404(a) and Item 308(a), the assessment belongs to the bank's own management, whoever performs the work.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the report covers those controls. But the service auditor reports on the provider; it does not assess the bank's ICFR.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the auditor attests to ICFR. But Section 404(b) attests to management's assessment; it does not perform it.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: the provider's management runs the controls day to day, but Section 404 puts the assessment on the user company's management, which may rely on a Type 2 report.

tips: Eliminate: C and B are auditors who report on someone else's work; neither performs the bank management's Section 404(a) assessment.
Final two: A beats D because outsourcing moves the processing, not the assessment; the SEC staff keeps it with the user company's management.
Exam cue: outsourced process, same owner; user-company management assesses, using a Type 2 report as evidence.

questions.subtopic: 5C2 Service organizations: from SAS 70 to SSAE 18. Report type
questions.question: A software company bills customers through a cloud platform run by a service organization, and management needs evidence that the platform's controls operated throughout the fiscal year. Which report BEST meets this need?

options.A: A SOC 2 report on security and availability criteria
options.B: The provider's signed letter stating its controls worked
options.C: A SOC 1 Type 1 report dated at fiscal year-end
options.D: A SOC 1 Type 2 report covering the fiscal year period

questions.key_concept: Only a SOC 1 Type 2 report tests whether controls relevant to ICFR operated effectively over a period.
questions.pre_read: Match two needs: controls relevant to financial reporting, and evidence of operation over time rather than design.
questions.correct_explanation: The SEC staff's FAQ describes a Type 2 report as including the service auditor's tests of whether controls operated effectively during a specified period; a Type 1 report speaks as of a date, without those tests. SOC 1 is the AICPA examination aimed at controls relevant to user entities' internal control over financial reporting. Management needs evidence of operation across the year, so a SOC 1 Type 2 report fits.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because security matters for a cloud platform. But SOC 2 reports on trust services criteria, not on controls relevant to user entities' ICFR.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it is quick to get. But a provider's own statement is not an independent service auditor's tested report on operating effectiveness.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: a SOC 1 Type 1 covers the right controls but only as of a date, without the period-long operating-effectiveness tests the SEC staff's FAQ ties to Type 2.

tips: Eliminate: A reports on trust services criteria rather than ICFR, and B is the provider vouching for itself without independent testing.
Final two: D beats C because the SEC staff's FAQ ties tests of operating effectiveness over a period to a Type 2 report; a Type 1 report speaks as of a date.
Exam cue: 'operated throughout the period' means Type 2; 'relevant to financial reporting' means SOC 1.

questions.subtopic: 5C2 Service organizations: from SAS 70 to SSAE 18. No evidence available
questions.question: A large accelerated filer's claims processor refuses to provide a Type 2 report or testing access, and management has no compensating controls. What is management's BEST course in its annual ICFR report?

options.A: Exclude the process and disclose the omission as a scope limitation
options.B: Judge whether the gap means ICFR must be concluded not effective
options.C: Leave the conclusion on that process to the auditor's attestation
options.D: Rely on the processor's written assurance that its controls work

questions.key_concept: Management's ICFR report cannot carry a scope limitation; an unassessable outsourced process may mean ICFR is not effective.
questions.pre_read: Recall what management's annual report must always state, and whether part of ICFR can be left out of it.
questions.correct_explanation: Item 308(a)(3) requires management's report to state whether ICFR is effective, and Release No. 33-8810 says the rules do not permit a management report with a scope limitation. Without a Type 2 report, access or compensating controls, management must decide whether the inability to assess the outsourced process is significant enough to conclude that ICFR is not effective. Neither an assurance letter nor the auditor fills that gap.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: carving out the process feels transparent, but the SEC says management's ICFR report may not carry a scope limitation.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the auditor attests under 404(b). But the attestation reports on management's assessment; it does not replace management's own conclusion.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it is evidence of a kind. But a provider's own assurance is not tested evidence of operating effectiveness, and no compensating controls exist.

tips: Eliminate: D accepts untested assurance from the provider and C hands management's conclusion to the auditor; neither is evidence management can stand on.
Final two: B beats A because the SEC's rules do not allow a management ICFR report with a scope limitation, so the gap must be judged.
Exam cue: management's ICFR report always concludes on effectiveness; apart from the SEC staff's narrow allowance for a newly acquired business, there is no scope-limitation exit.

questions.subtopic: 5A1 The original framework (1992). Who carries it out
questions.question: A SOX team lead compares COSO's definition of internal control, kept in the 2013 update, with Rule 13a-15(f). Under both, the process is effected by:

options.A: internal audit alone, acting on behalf of the audit committee
options.B: management alone, with the board approving policy
options.C: the board of directors, management and other personnel
options.D: the board, management, staff and the independent auditor

questions.key_concept: COSO's definition makes internal control a process effected by the entity's board, management and other personnel, not one function or an outsider.
questions.pre_read: Picture who carries out controls day to day and who oversees them, then ask who stands outside the company.
questions.correct_explanation: COSO defines internal control as a process effected by an entity's board of directors, management and other personnel, a definition the 2013 update kept, and Rule 13a-15(f) names the same three groups for ICFR. It is about people at every level, not one department. The independent auditor tests controls for its own report but does not effect the company's internal control, which is why D loses.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because internal audit evaluates controls. But COSO spreads the process across the board, management and other personnel, and SOX itself does not require an internal audit function.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because management designs and runs most controls. But COSO also names the board and other personnel; internal control is effected by people at every level.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: it names the right internal actors but adds the independent auditor, who tests controls for its own attestation and is not part of the company's internal control.

tips: Eliminate: A gives the whole process to one function, and B leaves out the board's oversight and the staff who run controls day to day.
Final two: C beats D because the independent auditor tests controls from outside; COSO's definition names only the entity's own board, management and other personnel.
Exam cue: COSO's 'effected by' is always board, management and other personnel, meaning people inside the entity at every level.

questions.subtopic: 5A1 The original framework (1992). Compliance controls in ICFR
questions.question: An issuer's SOX lead reviews a control over environmental permit terms and one over the SEC's financial statement form and content rules. Under Rule 13a-15(f) as Release 33-8238 explains it, which falls within ICFR?

options.A: Only the control over the SEC's financial statement rules
options.B: Both, since COSO's compliance objective covers all laws
options.C: Neither, because ICFR leaves out every compliance objective
options.D: Only the permit control, because breaches can bring fines

questions.key_concept: ICFR excludes COSO's operations and compliance objectives, except compliance with laws directly related to preparing the financial statements.
questions.pre_read: Ask which law governs how the financial statements themselves are prepared, and which governs the rest of the business.
questions.correct_explanation: Rule 13a-15(f) defines ICFR around reliable financial reporting. Release No. 33-8238 explains that the definition leaves out COSO's operations objectives and its compliance objectives, except compliance with laws directly related to preparing the financial statements, such as the SEC's financial reporting requirements. So the control over the SEC's form and content rules is in scope, and the permit control is not.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because COSO's compliance category spans all laws. But the SEC's ICFR is only the financial reporting slice, so general legal compliance stays outside.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: ICFR does drop most compliance objectives, but the SEC kept compliance with laws directly related to preparing the financial statements, such as its own reporting rules.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because fines affect the numbers. But recording a fine is a financial reporting control; the permit control itself serves a compliance objective outside ICFR.

tips: Eliminate: B carries COSO's whole compliance category into ICFR, and D treats a possible fine as turning the permit control into a financial reporting control.
Final two: A beats C because the SEC kept one compliance slice in ICFR: laws directly related to preparing the financial statements.
Exam cue: in ICFR, a compliance control counts only when the law governs the financial statements themselves.

questions.subtopic: 5A1 The original framework (1992). Warehouse access controls
questions.question: Under SEC Release No. 33-8238, how should management treat warehouse access controls for ICFR at a distributor that counts inventory once a year and prepares quarterly statements solely from perpetual records?

options.A: Within ICFR only after a theft has actually been detected
options.B: Outside ICFR, since COSO treats safeguarding as an operations goal
options.C: Outside ICFR, since safeguarding belongs to disclosure controls
options.D: Within ICFR, since interim figures rely on records a theft would distort

questions.key_concept: Safeguarding of assets is part of the SEC's ICFR, and physical controls count when the financial statements rely on the records they protect.
questions.pre_read: Ask what would catch a theft before the quarterly figures go out, and what the figures rest on in the meantime.
questions.correct_explanation: Rule 13a-15(f)(3) puts safeguarding of assets in ICFR where unauthorized use or disposition could materially affect the statements. Release No. 33-8238 (footnote 57, quoting COSO's 1992 report) notes that physical security over inventory, normally an operations control, also falls within financial reporting when management relies solely on perpetual records, as for interim reporting. No count would catch a theft before the quarterly figures go out, so the access controls are in scope.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because a loss makes the risk visible. But ICFR scope follows the risk that a theft distorts the figures, not whether one has happened yet.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: COSO placed safeguarding mainly under operations, but the SEC wrote it into ICFR, and here no count would catch a theft before quarter-end figures go out.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the two concepts overlap. But the SEC put safeguarding in the ICFR definition itself; a company may even design disclosure controls without it.

tips: Eliminate: A waits for an actual loss though scope follows risk, and C moves safeguarding out of ICFR into disclosure controls, the reverse of the SEC's definition.
Final two: D beats B because the SEC's ICFR definition includes safeguarding, and with no count before quarter-end the access controls protect the quarterly figures.
Exam cue: a control's category can change with reliance; physical security joins ICFR when the statements rely on records that a theft would leave wrong.

questions.subtopic: 5A2 The 2013 update. A sustainability report
questions.question: A company's sustainability team asks where COSO 2013 places controls over its voluntary, non-financial sustainability report. Which objective category MOST accurately fits?

options.A: Compliance, since the report is published to outside parties
options.B: Reporting, which the 2013 update widened beyond financial
options.C: None, since COSO 2013 covers financial statements alone
options.D: Operations, since COSO's reporting category is financial only

questions.key_concept: COSO 2013 widened the reporting objective to internal and external, financial and non-financial reporting.
questions.pre_read: Recall what the 2013 update changed on the objectives face of the cube, compared with the 1992 edition.
questions.correct_explanation: COSO's 2013 update widened the old financial reporting objective into a reporting category covering internal and external, financial and non-financial reporting. A voluntary sustainability report is external, non-financial reporting, so its controls sit in the reporting category. Treating reporting as financial only is the 1992 view.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the report goes to outsiders. But compliance objectives concern adherence to laws and regulations; publishing information is a reporting objective.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because SOX work centers on the financial statements. But COSO's framework spans operations, reporting and compliance, well beyond the statements.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: under the 1992 edition the reporting objective was financial reporting, but the 2013 update widened it to non-financial and internal reporting too.

tips: Eliminate: A confuses publishing to outsiders with obeying laws, and C narrows COSO to the SOX slice it is often used for.
Final two: B beats D because the 2013 update widened reporting to internal and external, financial and non-financial reports.
Exam cue: in 2013, 'financial reporting' became 'reporting'; non-financial or internal reports belong to the reporting objective.

questions.subtopic: 5A2 The 2013 update. Points of focus
questions.question: A SOX lead plans to rate a COSO 2013 principle as failed unless every listed point of focus under it is documented as in place. Which response BEST fits COSO's guidance?

options.A: Points of focus are aids; no separate assessment of each is required
options.B: Right, because points of focus replaced the principles in 2013
options.C: Right, because each point of focus is a required control
options.D: Each point of focus applies unless management documents why it does not

questions.key_concept: Points of focus help judge whether principles are present and functioning; COSO does not require assessing each one separately.
questions.pre_read: Rank the 2013 framework's layers: components, principles, then points of focus. Ask which layer carries the requirement.
questions.correct_explanation: COSO's FAQ (Question 4) calls points of focus typical characteristics of principles that help management judge whether a principle is present and functioning. The framework does not require management to assess each point of focus separately, and some may not suit every entity. Management still needs persuasive evidence that each relevant principle is present and functioning; a missing point of focus is not an automatic failure.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because both are listed together. But the 17 principles remain the requirements; points of focus sit beneath them as supporting characteristics.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because points of focus read like control steps. But COSO prescribes no specific controls; management chooses controls by judgment.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: it sounds prudent, but COSO sets no default that each point of focus applies; some may not suit the entity, and none must be assessed separately.

tips: Eliminate: B inverts the hierarchy, since principles stay the requirements, and C reads points of focus as mandated controls, which COSO does not prescribe.
Final two: A beats D because COSO says management need not assess points of focus separately, so no 'applies unless explained' default exists.
Exam cue: principles are required; points of focus are helpers. Effectiveness is judged at the principle and component level.

questions.subtopic: 5A2 The 2013 update. A new system and an acquisition
questions.question: Before moving to a new ERP system and closing an acquisition, a manufacturer's finance team studies how both could affect its internal control. Under COSO 2013, which principle does this MOST directly apply?

options.A: Principle 11, on general control activities over technology
options.B: Principle 16, on ongoing and separate evaluations
options.C: Principle 9, on identifying and analyzing significant change
options.D: Principle 3, on structures, reporting lines and authority

questions.key_concept: COSO 2013 principle 9 places the analysis of significant changes, such as new systems or acquisitions, under risk assessment.
questions.pre_read: Notice the timing: the team is looking ahead at changes, not testing controls already in place.
questions.correct_explanation: Principle 9, under risk assessment, has the organization spot and weigh changes in its business or technology that could materially alter how its internal control works. Studying the effect of an ERP move and an acquisition before they happen is that principle at work. General controls over technology (principle 11) matter once the new system runs, but they do not analyze the change itself or the acquisition.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the ERP system will need general controls over technology, but principle 11 covers those controls, not studying how a change, acquisition included, affects internal control.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because evaluations check controls. But principle 16 checks whether components are present and functioning; looking ahead at change is risk assessment.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because acquisitions change the organization chart. But principle 3 sets structures and authority; analyzing a change's effect on control is principle 9.

tips: Eliminate: B is monitoring of existing controls, and D is setting structure and authority; neither analyzes an upcoming change.
Final two: C beats A because the team is analyzing change before it happens, which is risk assessment's principle 9, and an acquisition is not a technology control.
Exam cue: new system or acquisition ahead? COSO files the analysis of change under risk assessment, principle 9.

questions.subtopic: 5A2 The 2013 update. A cyber example
questions.question: An online retailer's risk team applies COSO's 2015 paper 'COSO in the Cyber Age' to cyber risk. According to the paper, what should its cyber risk assessment address FIRST?

options.A: How to give every system the same strong protection
options.B: Which information systems matter most to its objectives
options.C: Which attackers are likely to target it, and their methods
options.D: Which firewall and access controls are already in place

questions.key_concept: COSO's cyber guidance starts the risk assessment from the information systems most valuable to the entity's objectives.
questions.pre_read: Think about the order of a risk assessment under COSO: objectives first, then risks to them, then controls.
questions.correct_explanation: COSO in the Cyber Age (2015) applies the 2013 framework to cyber risk and says the assessment should begin by understanding which information systems are valuable to the organization, measured by their impact on its objectives. Likely attackers and their methods are analyzed next, focused on those systems. Profiling attackers before knowing what matters leaves the team without a basis to set priorities.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it sounds thorough. But the paper warns that trying to protect everything overprotects some systems and underprotects others.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: the paper does analyze likely attackers and methods, but only after the organization knows which information systems are most valuable to its objectives.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because controls are concrete. But control activities follow the risk assessment; listing existing controls does not show what most needs protecting.

tips: Eliminate: A is the equal-protection approach the paper warns against, and D starts with control activities before any risk assessment.
Final two: B beats C because the paper begins with what is most valuable to objectives, then studies who would attack it and how.
Exam cue: COSO's order for cyber risk is critical systems first, threats next, layered controls after.

questions.subtopic: 5B1 ERM (2004) and how it differs from internal control. A currency risk decision
questions.question: A treasury team has assessed a currency risk and now weighs whether to accept, reduce, share or avoid it. In COSO's 2004 ERM framework, which component is this MOST directly?

options.A: Control activities
options.B: Event identification
options.C: Risk assessment
options.D: Risk response

questions.key_concept: In ERM 2004, risk response follows risk assessment and chooses whether to accept, reduce, share or avoid a risk.
questions.pre_read: Place the team's step in the 2004 ERM sequence: what came just before, and what comes next.
questions.correct_explanation: In the 2004 ERM framework, risk assessment follows event identification and comes before risk response, where the options (accept, reduce, share or avoid) are examined, costs and benefits weighed and a response chosen. The team has finished assessing and is now choosing, so this is risk response. Control activities are the policies and procedures that help carry out a chosen response; they follow the choice rather than make it.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: control activities help make sure risk responses are carried out, but choosing whether to accept, reduce, share or avoid a risk is the risk response component.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it is an early ERM step. But event identification finds potential events; this risk is already identified and assessed.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the team just finished it. But risk assessment measures and prioritizes risks; it comes before the response choice.

tips: Eliminate: B comes earliest, finding the events, and C measures the risk the team has already assessed.
Final two: D beats A because choosing among accept, reduce, share and avoid is the response itself; control activities then help carry it out.
Exam cue: ERM 2004 runs identify events, assess risks, respond, then control. 'Accept, reduce, share or avoid' signals risk response.

questions.subtopic: 5B1 ERM (2004) and how it differs from internal control. Appetite and tolerance
questions.question: A logistics firm's board says it accepts moderate risk to grow, and management then allows on-time delivery to fall up to 2% below target. Under COSO's 2004 ERM concepts, how are these BEST classified?

options.A: Both are risk responses, chosen after assessing each risk
options.B: The board's statement is tolerance; the delivery band is appetite
options.C: The board's statement is appetite; the delivery band is tolerance
options.D: Both are risk tolerances, set at different levels of the entity

questions.key_concept: Risk appetite is the broad amount of risk accepted in pursuit of value; risk tolerance is acceptable variation around a specific objective.
questions.pre_read: Compare the two statements' breadth: one covers the whole entity's risk-taking, the other one measurable target.
questions.correct_explanation: COSO's 2004 framework defines risk appetite as the amount of risk, on a broad level, an entity is willing to accept in pursuit of value; the board's statement is that broad limit. Risk tolerance applies appetite to a specific objective as the acceptable variation, measured in that objective's own units, so the 2% delivery band is a tolerance. Staying within tolerances keeps the entity within its appetite.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because both shape action. But responses are the accept, reduce, share or avoid choices for a risk; these statements set limits.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: it uses the right two terms but reverses them; appetite is the broad statement, and tolerance is the measurable band around one objective.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because both set limits. But the board's broad statement is not tied to one objective in its units, so it is appetite, not a tolerance.

tips: Eliminate: A confuses limits with the accept, reduce, share or avoid choices, and D treats a broad, entity-wide statement as tied to one objective.
Final two: C beats B because appetite is broad and strategic, while tolerance is the acceptable variation around a specific objective, in its own units.
Exam cue: a broad, entity-wide 'how much risk we accept' is appetite; a number around one target is tolerance.

questions.subtopic: 5B1 ERM (2004) and how it differs from internal control. Where objectives sit
questions.question: A SOX team maps the 2004 ERM framework's objective setting component onto COSO's 2013 internal control framework. Where does the internal control framework MOST directly address setting objectives?

options.A: In risk assessment, under principle 6 on specifying suitable objectives
options.B: In control environment, under principle 2 on board oversight
options.C: In monitoring activities, under principle 16 on separate evaluations
options.D: In a separate objective setting component, as in the ERM framework

questions.key_concept: Internal control treats objectives as a precondition within risk assessment (principle 6); ERM 2004 makes objective setting a separate component.
questions.pre_read: Count the internal control framework's components first, then find which component needs objectives before it can work.
questions.correct_explanation: The 2013 internal control framework has five components and no objective setting component. It treats objectives as a precondition to risk assessment: principle 6, under risk assessment, asks the organization to specify objectives clearly enough to identify and assess risks to them. ERM 2004 made objective setting its own component, one of the additions that make ERM broader than internal control.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the board oversees strategy. But principle 2 concerns the board's independence and oversight of internal control, not specifying objectives.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because evaluations compare results with criteria. But principle 16 checks whether components are present and functioning; it does not set objectives.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: ERM 2004 does make objective setting a component, but the internal control framework keeps five components and handles objectives through principle 6 in risk assessment.

tips: Eliminate: B is board oversight of internal control, and C is monitoring whether components function; neither specifies objectives.
Final two: A beats D because the internal control framework has only five components; objectives enter through principle 6, as a precondition to assessing risk.
Exam cue: objective setting is a component only in ERM 2004; in internal control it is principle 6, inside risk assessment.

questions.subtopic: 5B2 ERM (2017): strategy and performance. Where appetite is set
questions.question: A risk officer briefs the board on COSO's 2017 ERM framework. In that framework, defining risk appetite is a principle MOST directly placed in the component of:

options.A: Performance
options.B: Governance and culture
options.C: Information, communication and reporting
options.D: Strategy and objective-setting

questions.key_concept: ERM 2017 places defining risk appetite (principle 7) in the strategy and objective-setting component.
questions.pre_read: Recall which ERM 2017 component holds the principles about choosing strategy and setting business objectives.
questions.correct_explanation: COSO's 2017 framework lists Defines Risk Appetite as principle 7, in the strategy and objective-setting component, alongside analyzing business context, evaluating alternative strategies and formulating business objectives. Appetite is set with strategy so it can guide which strategy to pursue. The board oversees risk under governance and culture, but the appetite principle itself sits in strategy and objective-setting.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because performance prioritizes risks against appetite. But it uses an appetite already defined; it does not set one.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: the board's risk oversight is principle 1 under governance and culture, but defining risk appetite is principle 7, under strategy and objective-setting.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because appetite must be communicated. But this component covers information systems, communication and reporting, not defining appetite.

tips: Eliminate: A applies an appetite already set when prioritizing risks, and C communicates risk information rather than defining limits.
Final two: D beats B because ERM 2017 sets appetite together with strategy (principle 7); governance and culture holds the board's oversight role.
Exam cue: in ERM 2017, appetite is born in strategy and objective-setting, then used in performance to prioritize risks.

questions.subtopic: 5B2 ERM (2017): strategy and performance. What ERM is
questions.question: A CEO plans to declare ERM in place once a new risk department keeps a register of every enterprise risk. Under COSO's 2017 ERM framework, which response is MOST accurate?

options.A: Not yet; the risk department must also report quarterly to the board
options.B: Not yet; ERM is culture, capabilities and practices tied to strategy
options.C: Yes; a complete inventory of enterprise risks meets the framework
options.D: Yes, once internal audit certifies the register each year

questions.key_concept: COSO 2017 describes ERM as culture, capabilities and practices integrated with strategy, not a department, a risk list or a checklist.
questions.pre_read: Ask what COSO's 2017 summary says ERM is not, before deciding what would make it real.
questions.correct_explanation: COSO's 2017 executive summary clears up misconceptions: ERM is not a function or department, and it is more than a risk listing. It is the culture, capabilities and practices an organization integrates with strategy-setting and applies in carrying out that strategy, to manage risk in creating, preserving and realizing value. A department and a register can support ERM, but on their own they do not make it.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: reporting to the board is useful, but it still treats ERM as a department's task; COSO says ERM is not a function or department.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because a full risk list looks thorough. But COSO says ERM is more than a risk listing and needs practices that actively manage risk.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because certification sounds rigorous. But COSO says ERM is not a checklist, and a yearly sign-off creates neither culture nor practices.

tips: Eliminate: C treats a risk listing as ERM, and D treats a yearly sign-off as ERM; COSO's 2017 summary corrects both misconceptions.
Final two: B beats A because COSO says ERM is not a function or department, so better reporting by the department still misses what ERM is.
Exam cue: an option that makes ERM a department, a list or a checklist repeats a misconception COSO's 2017 summary corrects.

questions.subtopic: 5B2 ERM (2017): strategy and performance. Limits by business line
questions.question: A bank's three business lines each stay within their own credit limits, but nobody combines their exposures against the board's risk appetite. Under COSO's 2017 ERM framework, which principle is MOST clearly missing?

options.A: Assesses substantial change, in review and revision
options.B: Develops portfolio view, in the performance component
options.C: Defines risk appetite, in strategy and objective-setting
options.D: Exercises board risk oversight, in governance and culture

questions.key_concept: ERM 2017's portfolio view (principle 14) looks at total risk across the entity against risk appetite, not unit by unit.
questions.pre_read: Separate what already exists in the scenario from what nobody is doing yet.
questions.correct_explanation: Principle 14, Develops Portfolio View, sits in the performance component: after identifying, assessing, prioritizing and responding to risks, the organization looks at the total amount of risk it has assumed. Each business line staying within its own limits does not show whether their combined exposure fits the board's risk appetite; only an entity-wide portfolio view does. The appetite already exists, so principle 7 is not the gap.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because exposures can shift. But principle 15 covers identifying substantial changes; the gap is combining existing exposures.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: appetite matters here, but the board has already set one; what is missing is the combined, entity-wide view to compare with it.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the board is involved. But board oversight works only once management builds the combined view the board needs.

tips: Eliminate: A is about spotting substantial change, and D is the board's oversight role; neither combines exposures across business lines.
Final two: B beats C because an appetite already exists; what nobody does is view the total risk across units, which is principle 14.
Exam cue: units fine one by one, total unknown? That is the portfolio view, principle 14 in performance.

questions.subtopic: 5C1 Software and spreadsheets. Scoping IT
questions.question: An issuer's SOX team scopes IT for its annual ICFR evaluation. Under SEC Release No. 33-8810, identifying risks and controls within IT should be:

options.A: performed yearly as an IT audit by the internal audit function
options.B: limited to systems bought from outside software vendors
options.C: run as a separate IT evaluation after business process scoping
options.D: built into management's top-down, risk-based approach to ICFR

questions.key_concept: Under Release No. 33-8810, IT risks and controls are identified within management's top-down, risk-based approach, not separately.
questions.pre_read: Ask why IT is part of an ICFR evaluation at all, and what that implies for when it is scoped.
questions.correct_explanation: Release No. 33-8810 says the identification of risks and controls within IT should not be a separate evaluation; it should be an integral part of management's top-down, risk-based approach to identifying risks and controls and deciding what evidence it needs. IT is in scope because controls that address financial reporting risks depend on it, so it is assessed with those risks, not afterwards on its own track.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because internal audit often tests IT. But SOX does not require an internal audit function, and the evaluation is management's, scoped top-down.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because purchased systems can feel riskier. But scope follows the financial reporting risk a control addresses, whether the software was bought or built.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: many teams do run IT on a separate track, but the SEC's guidance says IT risks and controls are identified within the top-down approach, not separately.

tips: Eliminate: A assumes a SOX internal audit requirement that does not exist, and B scopes IT by how software was acquired rather than by risk.
Final two: D beats C because Release No. 33-8810 puts IT risk and control identification inside the top-down, risk-based approach, not in a separate evaluation.
Exam cue: in SEC guidance IT is never its own island; it is in scope because, and to the extent that, financial reporting controls depend on it.

questions.subtopic: 5C1 Software and spreadsheets. A duplicate-payment review
questions.question: Under SEC Release No. 33-8810, what should management's evaluation consider when an accounts payable supervisor investigates each item on a system-generated report of possible duplicate payments?

options.A: The manual review and the IT controls behind the report
options.B: The manual review alone, since a person performs the control
options.C: Only the report's original validation, done when it was built
options.D: The report's automated logic alone, since the system flags each duplicate

questions.key_concept: A manual control that relies on a system report brings the report's application and IT general controls into management's evaluation.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the supervisor's review depends on to catch every duplicate payment.
questions.correct_explanation: Release No. 33-8810 says controls may be automated, depend on IT, or combine manual and automated steps, giving a person investigating items on a computer-generated exception report as an example. Management's evaluation then considers the manual step and the IT-dependent application controls and relevant IT general controls that make the report reliable. A careful review of an incomplete report would still miss duplicates.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: the supervisor's review is the visible control, but it works only if the system's report is complete and accurate, so the IT behind it is evaluated too.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the report was checked once. But it keeps working only if IT general controls over changes and access operate, so a one-time check is not enough.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the system flags the items. But the supervisor's investigation is part of the control, and the logic stays reliable only with IT general controls behind it.

tips: Eliminate: C relies on a one-time check at build, and D drops both the supervisor's step and the IT general controls behind the logic.
Final two: A beats B because a manual review of a system report depends on the report being complete and accurate, so the IT behind it is in scope too.
Exam cue: manual control using a system report? Evaluate both the person's step and the IT that produces the report.
