questions.subtopic: 5C1 Software and spreadsheets. Choosing among controls
questions.question: Under SEC Release No. 33-8810, which statement about management's evaluation is MOST accurate when a manual reconciliation and an automated three-way match each fully address the same receivables risk and IT general controls tested effective?

options.A: Management must pick the manual one, as SEC guidance prefers people's review
options.B: Management must fully retest the automated match every quarter
options.C: Management may evaluate just the control that is more efficient to test
options.D: Management must evaluate both, since each one addresses the risk

questions.key_concept: When several controls each address a risk, management may evaluate the one whose operating evidence it can obtain most efficiently.
questions.pre_read: Notice that both controls fully address the risk, and note what the general controls' results allow.
questions.correct_explanation: Release No. 33-8810 (Section II.A.1.b) says that when more than one control adequately addresses a financial reporting risk, management may select the control whose operating effectiveness it can evaluate more efficiently. It adds that when IT general controls are effective, automated controls may be more efficient to evaluate than manual ones. Evaluating both is allowed, but no rule says management must, so every 'must' option fails.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because manual reviews feel robust. But the SEC states no preference for manual controls; with effective general controls, automated ones may be more efficient.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because automated logic can change. But the release sets no quarterly full-retest rule; effective IT general controls support relying on the automated match.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: management may evaluate both, but it need not; the SEC's guidance lets it select the control whose evidence is more efficient to obtain.

tips: Eliminate: A invents an SEC preference for manual controls, and B invents a quarterly full-retest rule the release does not contain.
Final two: C beats D because nothing makes management evaluate both; the SEC lets it pick the control whose evidence is more efficient to evaluate.
Exam cue: two controls, one risk? SEC guidance lets management test the more efficient one; effective general controls often make that the automated control.

questions.subtopic: 5C1 Software and spreadsheets. A forecasting spreadsheet
questions.question: A retailer's HR team keeps a staffing-forecast spreadsheet that feeds no journal entry, estimate, disclosure or control over financial reporting. For Section 404, how should management BEST treat it?

options.A: In scope, as COSO 2013 also covers operations objectives
options.B: In scope, since every spreadsheet needs access and change controls
options.C: Outside ICFR once IT confirms it is not a system of record
options.D: Outside ICFR, since it poses no financial reporting risk

questions.key_concept: A spreadsheet that feeds nothing in the financial statements carries no financial reporting risk and falls outside ICFR.
questions.pre_read: Trace where the spreadsheet's output goes, and whether any of it reaches the financial statements.
questions.correct_explanation: Scope follows financial reporting risk. Rule 13a-15(f) defines ICFR by reliable financial reporting, and Release No. 33-8810 has management evaluate the controls that address financial reporting risks, not those serving only operations. A staffing forecast that feeds no entry, estimate or disclosure carries no financial reporting risk, so it stays outside the Section 404 assessment, even though COSO's wider framework covers operations.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: COSO 2013 does cover operations objectives, but the SEC's ICFR is only the financial reporting slice, so an operations-only tool stays outside Section 404.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because spreadsheet controls are good practice. But Section 404 scope follows financial reporting risk, not the file type.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it sounds procedural. But system-of-record labels do not set SOX scope; financial reporting risk does, in any tool.

tips: Eliminate: B scopes by file type and C scopes by an IT label; SOX scope follows financial reporting risk instead.
Final two: D beats A because the SEC's ICFR leaves out COSO's operations objectives, and this spreadsheet touches no amount or disclosure in the statements.
Exam cue: the same test works both ways; a tool feeding the statements is in scope however it is built, and a tool feeding nothing in them is out.

questions.subtopic: 5C2 Service organizations: from SAS 70 to SSAE 18. Today's standard
questions.question: A payroll processor engages a service auditor to issue a SOC 1 report for its user entities. Today, the service auditor MOST accurately performs that examination under:

options.A: SSAE No. 18 as amended, codified in AT-C section 320
options.B: AU-C section 402, on audits of entities using service organizations
options.C: SSAE No. 16, as a stand-alone attestation standard
options.D: SAS No. 70, as the auditing standard for these reports

questions.key_concept: Service auditors now examine SOC 1 engagements under SSAE No. 18 (AT-C section 320); SAS 70 and SSAE No. 16 are history.
questions.pre_read: Separate the service auditor's standard from the user auditor's, then ask which edition is current.
questions.correct_explanation: The AICPA says SOC 1 reports were formerly known as SAS 70 reports, and that SSAE No. 18 addresses a service auditor's examination of controls at a service organization relevant to user entities. SSAE No. 18 recodified the attestation standards and superseded SSAE Nos. 10 to 17 (except No. 15), which takes in SSAE No. 16. The AICPA's SOC 1 guide places the examination under AT-C section 320.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting, but AU-C section 402 guides a nonissuer's auditor whose client uses a service organization; an issuer's auditor follows PCAOB standards. Neither governs the service auditor.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: SSAE No. 16 is an earlier attestation standard, but SSAE No. 18 recodified and superseded SSAE Nos. 10 to 17, except No. 15.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because older SEC guidance says 'Type 2 SAS 70 report'. But the AICPA says SOC 1 reports were formerly known as SAS 70 reports; that name is history.

tips: Eliminate: D is the name SOC 1 reports used to carry, and B is a nonissuer user auditor's standard, not the service auditor's.
Final two: A beats C because SSAE No. 18 recodified and superseded the earlier SSAEs, No. 16 included; SOC 1 work now sits in AT-C section 320.
Exam cue: service auditor, SSAE No. 18 (AT-C 320); a nonissuer's auditor, AU-C 402; 'SAS 70' in older guidance means today's SOC 1.

questions.subtopic: 5C2 Service organizations: from SAS 70 to SSAE 18. After a clean report
questions.question: A manufacturer's payroll provider supplies a clean SOC 1 Type 2 report covering the full fiscal year. For its ICFR assessment, management MOST clearly remains responsible for:

options.A: re-performing the service auditor's tests of the provider's controls
options.B: controls over the data it sends to and receives from the provider
options.C: filing the SOC 1 report with the SEC alongside its Form 10-K
options.D: nothing further, since the report covers the outsourced process

questions.key_concept: Relying on a service auditor's Type 2 report leaves management responsible for controls over data sent to and received from the provider.
questions.pre_read: Picture the payroll data's round trip and ask which part the provider's report cannot see.
questions.correct_explanation: The SEC staff says management keeps the responsibility to assess controls over outsourced operations and may rely on a service auditor's Type 2 report, but remains responsible for maintaining and evaluating controls over the flow of information to and from the service organization. A clean report speaks to the provider's controls, not to whether the manufacturer's own payroll inputs and the results it records are complete and accurate.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it sounds thorough. But the staff lets management rely on the Type 2 report; re-performing the service auditor's tests is not required.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the report supports the annual assessment. But no rule requires filing a SOC 1 report with the SEC; management keeps it as evidence.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: a full-year Type 2 report is strong evidence on the provider, but the SEC staff says management still owns controls over information flowing to and from it.

tips: Eliminate: A redoes work the staff lets management rely on, and C adds an SEC filing no rule requires.
Final two: B beats D because even with a clean Type 2 report, management keeps controls over what it sends to and receives from the provider.
Exam cue: a SOC 1 report covers the provider's side; the user company keeps its own controls at the handoffs.

questions.subtopic: 5C2 Service organizations: from SAS 70 to SSAE 18. Relying on a Type 2 report
questions.question: A retailer's management engaged its own independent auditor to prepare a Type 2 report on its payroll provider's controls. Under the SEC staff's ICFR FAQ, which answer BEST settles whether management may rely on it?

options.A: Yes; reliance is allowed when one firm audits both companies
options.B: Yes; its own auditor's Type 2 report tests a full period
options.C: No; the company's own auditor wrote it at management's request
options.D: No; management needs a SOC 2 report for this purpose instead

questions.key_concept: Management may not rely on a Type 2 report that it engaged its own audit firm to prepare on the service organization.
questions.pre_read: Note who engaged the service auditor and for whom, not just what kind of report was issued.
questions.correct_explanation: The SEC staff's ICFR FAQ (Question 8) lets management rely on a provider's Type 2 report even when one firm audits both companies. But if management engages its own audit firm to prepare that report, management cannot rely on it for its ICFR assessment, so it needs other evidence. The 2007 FAQ says "Type 2 SAS 70 report"; today that is a SOC 1 Type 2 report under SSAE No. 18.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the staff does allow reliance when the same firm audits both companies, but not when management itself engaged its own audit firm to prepare the report.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because Type 2 reports test operating effectiveness. But the staff bars reliance on a report management had its own audit firm prepare, whatever its content.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because SOC 2 sounds more thorough. But SOC 2 addresses trust services criteria; a SOC 1 Type 2 report is the one relevant to ICFR.

tips: Eliminate: B looks only at the report type, not who commissioned it, and D swaps in SOC 2, which addresses trust services criteria rather than ICFR.
Final two: C beats A because one firm auditing both companies is allowed, but management engaging its own audit firm to prepare the report is not.

questions.subtopic: 5A1 The original framework (1992). Where the framework came from
questions.question: A compliance team's trainer explains why COSO wrote its 1992 internal control framework. According to the SEC's account in Release No. 33-8238, the framework MOST directly answered:

options.A: the Sarbanes-Oxley Act's call for a framework for Section 404 reports
options.B: the Treadway Commission's call for a common control reference point
options.C: the PCAOB's request for criteria to use in audits of internal control
options.D: the internal accounting control duty the FCPA imposed in 1977

questions.key_concept: COSO's 1992 framework grew out of the Treadway Commission's 1987 recommendation that its sponsors build a common internal control reference point.
questions.pre_read: Put the events in date order: which bodies and laws existed before 1992, and which came a decade later?
questions.correct_explanation: Release No. 33-8238 recounts that the National Commission on Fraudulent Financial Reporting, known as the Treadway Commission, formed in 1985 and in 1987 urged its sponsoring organizations to integrate internal control concepts into a common reference point. Their committee, COSO, answered with the 1992 framework. The FCPA had required internal accounting controls since 1977, but it set a legal duty rather than asking for a shared framework.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because SOX made COSO central to Section 404 work. But the Act dates from 2002, a decade after COSO published its framework.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because auditors use frameworks as criteria. But the PCAOB was created by the 2002 Act; it did not exist when COSO wrote the 1992 framework.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: the FCPA did require internal accounting controls from 1977, but the call for one common framework came from the Treadway Commission's 1987 report.

tips: Eliminate: A and C. Both the Sarbanes-Oxley Act and the PCAOB date from 2002, ten years after COSO published its framework.
Final two: B beats D because the FCPA imposed a control duty, while the Treadway Commission asked its sponsors for one common reference point, which became COSO 1992.
Exam cue: COSO is the Committee of Sponsoring Organizations of the Treadway Commission; the name tells you where the framework came from.

questions.subtopic: 5B2 ERM (2017): strategy and performance. Directors and management
questions.question: A risk officer briefs new directors on COSO's 2017 ERM framework. Under its executive summary, the board's risk oversight role MOST directly includes:

options.A: holding overall responsibility for managing risk across the entity
options.B: choosing the risk response for each risk the business lines report
options.C: certifying the entity's risk appetite to the SEC in its annual report
options.D: reviewing, challenging and concurring on strategy and risk appetite

questions.key_concept: Under ERM 2017, management holds overall responsibility for managing risk; the board oversees by reviewing, challenging and concurring on strategy and appetite.
questions.pre_read: Separate who runs enterprise risk management day to day from who oversees it.
questions.correct_explanation: COSO's 2017 executive summary lists the board's risk oversight role as including reviewing, challenging and concurring with management on proposed strategy and risk appetite, on alignment with mission and values, and on significant decisions such as acquisitions. The same summary gives management overall responsibility for managing risk to the entity. The board oversees and challenges; management runs enterprise risk management and selects responses.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: someone must own entity-wide risk, but the executive summary gives management overall responsibility for managing risk; the board oversees and challenges it.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because directors care about responses. But selecting risk responses is principle 13 in the performance component, carried out by management.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because SOX links boards and SEC filings. But COSO's framework is voluntary guidance; nothing in it has the board certify appetite to the SEC.

tips: Eliminate: B and C. Selecting risk responses is management's work in the performance component, and COSO's framework creates no SEC certification.
Final two: D beats A because the 2017 executive summary gives management overall responsibility for managing risk; the board reviews, challenges and concurs.
Exam cue: in ERM 2017, management runs risk and the board oversees it; 'review, challenge, concur' are the board's verbs.

questions.subtopic: 5C1 Software and spreadsheets. A late system change
questions.question: A distributor's finance team moves its billing system to a new cloud platform six weeks before fiscal year-end. Under the SEC staff's 2005 ICFR statement, which treatment in this year's assessment is MOST accurate?

options.A: Include it; the staff allows no exclusion for late system changes
options.B: Exclude it for up to one year, as for an acquired business
options.C: Exclude it if management discloses the omission as a scope limitation
options.D: Include it if the independent auditor plans to test it this year

questions.key_concept: The SEC staff gives no scope exclusion for IT systems implemented late in the year; management plans and tests their controls in advance.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether the relief for a business acquired during the year also covers a system the company changes itself.
questions.correct_explanation: The SEC staff's May 2005 statement refused to let management exclude new IT systems or upgrades from its ICFR assessment, even when put in late in the year, rejecting the analogy to acquired businesses. Management can plan and test controls before go-live, since not all testing must happen at year-end. The one-year FAQ exclusion covers acquired businesses only. The Commission kept that position in its 2007 guidance, Release No. 33-8810.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: the staff's FAQ does let management exclude a business acquired during the year, but the 2005 statement refused to extend that relief to new IT systems.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because disclosure feels like a fair cure. But the staff gave no exclusion for system changes, so disclosure cannot take the new system out of scope.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because auditors focus on key systems. But scope follows management's own assessment duty; the new system is in it whatever the independent auditor plans.

tips: Eliminate: C and D. Disclosure cannot remove a system from the assessment, and management's scope does not depend on the independent auditor's test plan.
Final two: A beats B because the one-year relief covers acquired businesses; the 2005 staff statement refused the same treatment for new systems.
Exam cue: a business acquired late in the year may qualify for a one-year exclusion; a system changed late in the year does not.

questions.subtopic: 5A1 The original framework (1992). Audit committee oversight
questions.question: Under Release No. 33-8238's account of the 1992 COSO Report, which component holds the audit committee's oversight of financial reporting, such as challenging management's estimates?

options.A: Monitoring, since directors evaluate whether controls keep working
options.B: Information and communication, since filings go to regulators
options.C: Control environment, where the board's governance role sits
options.D: Risk assessment, since estimates carry a risk of misstatement

questions.key_concept: COSO treats the board's and audit committee's oversight of financial reporting as a key aspect of the control environment.
questions.pre_read: Ask which component holds the committee's role: governing, informing, analyzing risk or checking that controls work.
questions.correct_explanation: Release No. 33-8238 notes that the COSO Report treats the composition of the board and audit committee, and how directors carry out their financial reporting duties, as key aspects of the control environment, including overseeing the reporting process and assessing management's judgments and estimates. COSO's 2013 summary still places the board's governance oversight in the control environment. Monitoring evaluates whether components work; it is not where governance sits.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: directors do receive monitoring results, but the COSO Report counts the board's and audit committee's oversight among the key aspects of the control environment.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the committee reviews key filings. But that review is part of its oversight role, which the COSO Report places in the control environment.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because estimates carry risk. But analyzing that risk is management's risk assessment; the committee's challenge of estimates is governance oversight.

tips: Eliminate: B and D. Reviewing filings and challenging estimates are part of the committee's oversight, not the information flow itself or management's risk analysis.
Final two: C beats A because the COSO Report counts board and audit committee oversight as a key aspect of the control environment; monitoring evaluates controls.
Exam cue: who governs and sets the tone, such as the board, audit committee, ethics and structure, points to the control environment.

questions.subtopic: 5B1 ERM (2004) and how it differs from internal control. The cube's side face
questions.question: A risk manager sketches COSO's 2004 ERM cube for the risk committee, with the four objective categories across the top. Which labels BEST belong on the cube's side face?

options.A: Entity level, division, business unit and subsidiary
options.B: Internal environment, objective setting and event identification
options.C: The response options of accept, reduce, share and avoid
options.D: Governance and culture, performance, and review and revision

questions.key_concept: The 2004 ERM cube shows four objective categories, eight components and the entity's levels: entity-level, division, business unit and subsidiary.
questions.pre_read: Recall what each face of the cube shows: what the entity aims for, what it needs, and where it applies.
questions.correct_explanation: As COSO's 2011 paper Embracing ERM shows, the 2004 ERM cube sets the four objective categories (strategic, operations, reporting and compliance) across the top, the eight components down the front, and the entity's levels on the side: entity-level, division, business unit and subsidiary. The side face shows that ERM applies at every level of the organization. Internal environment, objective setting and event identification are components, so they belong on the front face.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: these are three of the eight 2004 ERM components, which run down the cube's front face, not its side.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because ERM 2004 names these four responses. But they are options within the risk response component, not a face of the cube.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because these are ERM component names. But they come from COSO's 2017 update, not from the 2004 cube, whose eight components run down its front face.

tips: Eliminate: C and D. Accept, reduce, share and avoid are response options, and governance and culture belongs to the 2017 update, not the 2004 cube.
Final two: A beats B because the eight components run down the front face; the side face shows the entity's levels, from entity-level to subsidiary.
Exam cue: on COSO's cubes, the third face is the organization's structure, its levels or units, never components or objectives.

questions.subtopic: 5A2 The 2013 update. Reading the updated cube
questions.question: A controller explains the cube in COSO's 2013 internal control framework to the new SOX team. In COSO's description, the five components MOST accurately represent:

options.A: what the entity strives to achieve in its operations
options.B: the steps of a serial process, performed one after another
options.C: what is required for the entity to achieve its objectives
options.D: the operating units and legal entities the system covers

questions.key_concept: In COSO's 2013 cube, objectives are what an entity strives for, components what it needs to achieve them, and structure where they apply.

questions.correct_explanation: COSO's 2013 executive summary describes a direct relationship in its cube: objectives are what an entity strives to achieve, components are what is required to achieve them, and the organizational structure is the third dimension. wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: what the entity strives to achieve describes the objectives, the cube's columns, of which operations is one category; the components are what is needed to achieve them.

wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the cube does show structure. But operating units and legal entities form its third dimension, not the components.

tips: Eliminate: B and D. COSO rejects a step-by-step reading of the components, and units and legal entities are the cube's third dimension.

questions.subtopic: 5B2 ERM (2017): strategy and performance. Expected conduct
questions.question: A consumer lender rewards branch staff for loan volume however they treat risk, so the board asks management to spell out the conduct it expects. Under COSO's 2017 ERM framework, which principle MOST directly applies?

options.A: Implements risk responses, in the performance component
options.B: Defines desired culture, in the governance and culture component
options.C: Communicates risk information, in information, communication and reporting
options.D: Demonstrates commitment to core values, in governance and culture

wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: core values sit in the same component, but principle 4 is commitment to the values held; spelling out the behaviors expected of staff is principle 3.

questions.subtopic: 5A1 The original framework (1992). Testing a framework's suitability
questions.question: Under Release No. 33-8238, which suitability criterion MOST clearly fails when an issuer's CFO finds a published control framework so vague that two evaluators testing the same controls reach different conclusions?

options.A: Freedom from bias in how the framework judges controls
options.B: Relevance to evaluating internal control over financial reporting
options.C: Completeness, so no factor that alters a conclusion is left out
options.D: Reasonably consistent measurements of a company's internal control

questions.key_concept: Release No. 33-8238 requires a suitable framework to be free from bias, allow consistent measurement, be sufficiently complete and be relevant to ICFR.
questions.pre_read: Name what goes wrong when two evaluators use the framework: a slant, a gap, irrelevance, or scatter.
questions.correct_explanation: Release No. 33-8238 says a suitable framework must be free from bias, permit reasonably consistent qualitative and quantitative measurements of a company's internal control, be sufficiently complete so that relevant factors that would alter a conclusion are not omitted, and be relevant to evaluating ICFR. Criteria so vague that evaluators reach different conclusions on the same controls fail the consistency test.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because inconsistent results look unfair. But bias means criteria slanted toward a result; vague criteria produce scatter, not a slant.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because suitability starts with relevance. But nothing suggests the framework addresses something other than ICFR; its problem is that two evaluators cannot apply it the same way.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: completeness asks whether relevant factors are left out; here the factors exist but are too vague to measure the same way twice.

tips: Eliminate: A and B. Nothing suggests the criteria lean toward one result or cover the wrong subject; the trouble is how they measure.
Final two: D beats C because the criteria are present but vague; completeness concerns factors left out, consistency concerns measuring the same controls the same way.
Exam cue: a suitable framework under Release No. 33-8238 is unbiased, consistent, complete and relevant; match the flaw to one of the four.

questions.subtopic: 5B1 ERM (2004) and how it differs from internal control. Rating before responses
questions.question: A procurement team rates a supplier-failure exposure as if the company had no backup suppliers or other responses in place. Under COSO's 2004 ERM framework, which term MOST accurately describes this rating?

options.A: Residual risk, the risk that remains after management responds
options.B: Speed of onset, how quickly the exposure could affect the company
options.C: Event identification, finding events that could affect objectives
options.D: Inherent risk, the risk before any action management might take

questions.key_concept: COSO's 2004 ERM framework defines inherent risk as risk absent management's actions and residual risk as what remains after its response.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether the rating counts the company's backup suppliers and other responses or assumes none exist.
questions.correct_explanation: COSO's 2004 ERM framework, as its 2012 paper Risk Assessment in Practice explains, defines inherent risk as the risk to an entity in the absence of any actions management might take to alter its likelihood or impact, and residual risk as the risk remaining after management's response. Rating the exposure as if no backup suppliers existed, before choosing a response, measures inherent risk.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: residual risk is the other half of the pair, but it is measured after management's response; this team rated the exposure as if no response existed.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because speed of onset is a common rating dimension. But it measures how fast a risk could arrive, not whether responses are counted.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the team is studying an exposure. But event identification finds events that could affect objectives; rating their size comes later, in risk assessment.

tips: Eliminate: B and C. Speed of onset measures how fast a risk could arrive, and event identification finds risks rather than rating them.
Final two: D beats A because residual risk counts management's responses; the team assumed none, which is inherent risk.
Exam cue: before responses, inherent risk; after responses, residual risk.

questions.subtopic: 5A1 The original framework (1992). A home-country framework
questions.question: A foreign-incorporated issuer that files Form 10-K evaluates ICFR against a recognized home-country framework that calls for no overall effectiveness conclusion. Under Release No. 33-8238, management's annual ICFR report must still:

options.A: state affirmatively whether ICFR is effective or not effective
options.B: follow the home framework and omit any overall conclusion
options.C: limit its conclusion to controls the home framework addresses
options.D: leave the effectiveness conclusion to the independent auditor's report

questions.key_concept: A home-country framework may be used, but management must still state affirmatively whether ICFR is effective.
questions.pre_read: Separate what the chosen framework asks for from what the SEC's rule requires in management's report.
questions.correct_explanation: Release No. 33-8238 notes that some home-country frameworks used for foreign companies do not require a statement on whether internal control is effective. Management relying on such a framework must still state affirmatively whether ICFR is, or is not, effective, as Item 308(a)(3) requires of every management report. The choice of framework cannot remove the SEC's required conclusion.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: the home framework sets the evaluation criteria, but the SEC's rules still require an affirmative statement on whether ICFR is effective.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the framework sets the evaluation's terms. But the conclusion covers ICFR as a whole, whatever the home framework addresses.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the independent auditor also reports on ICFR. But Item 308(a)(3) asks for management's own statement in management's report.

tips: Eliminate: C and D. The conclusion covers ICFR as a whole, and it belongs in management's own report, not the independent auditor's.
Final two: A beats B because Release No. 33-8238 says a home framework without an effectiveness statement does not excuse one; management must state it.
Exam cue: whatever framework is used, management's report says ICFR is effective or not effective.

questions.subtopic: 5B2 ERM (2017): strategy and performance. Before choosing a strategy
questions.question: Before choosing its strategy, a pharmacy chain's management studies how new drug-pricing rules, competitor mergers and changing customer habits could shift its risk profile. Under COSO's 2017 ERM framework, which principle is this MOST directly?

options.A: Assesses substantial change, a review and revision principle
options.B: Identifies risk, in the performance component
options.C: Analyzes business context, in strategy and objective-setting
options.D: Formulates business objectives, in strategy and objective-setting

questions.key_concept: ERM 2017 principle 6, analyzes business context, considers how business context could affect the risk profile, within strategy and objective-setting.
questions.pre_read: Note when the study happens: before a strategy is chosen, or after strategy and objectives are in place.
questions.correct_explanation: COSO's 2017 framework lists Analyzes Business Context as principle 6, in strategy and objective-setting: the organization considers the potential effects of business context on its risk profile. Studying regulation, competitors and customers before choosing a strategy is that analysis. Assessing substantial change, principle 15, sits in review and revision and looks for changes that could affect strategy and business objectives already set.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the facts involve change, but principle 15 reviews changes that could affect strategy and objectives already set; this study comes before strategy is chosen.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because risks are being studied. But identifying risk, principle 10, looks at risks to the performance of a chosen strategy and its business objectives.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it sits in the same component. But principle 9 sets business objectives that support a strategy already chosen; studying the outside world before choosing is principle 6.

tips: Eliminate: B and D. Identifying risk and formulating business objectives both work from a strategy already chosen; neither studies the outside world before the choice.
Final two: C beats A because the study comes before the strategy is chosen; principle 15 deals with change once strategy and objectives exist.
Exam cue: in ERM 2017, the outside world studied before choosing strategy is business context, principle 6.

questions.subtopic: 5A2 The 2013 update. Effect on the 404 reports
questions.question: In 2014, an accelerated filer's SOX team moved from COSO's 1992 framework to the 2013 update. According to COSO's FAQ, how would the move affect management's Section 404(a) assertion and the independent auditor's 404(b) attestation?

options.A: Management had to add a statement on each of the 17 principles
options.B: Management had to restate last year's assessment under the 2013 update
options.C: The auditor's 404(b) attestation became optional for that year
options.D: No change expected; management assessed how it applied the principles

questions.key_concept: COSO expected the 2013 update to leave Section 404(a) and 404(b) assertions unchanged; management assesses how its system applies the 17 principles.
questions.pre_read: Separate what the framework changes in management's work from what the SEC's rules ask the report to say.
questions.correct_explanation: COSO's 2013 FAQ, Question 5, says management's assertion on ICFR under Section 404(a) and 404(b) is not expected to change. To transition, senior management assesses how the company's system of internal control applies the 17 principles, and the board oversees that work. Item 308(a) asks for one overall conclusion on ICFR; it calls for no statement on each principle.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the 17 principles do drive the transition work, but COSO expects no change to the SOX assertions, and Item 308(a) asks for one overall conclusion.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because a new edition invites comparisons. But Item 308(a) assesses ICFR as of the latest fiscal year-end only, and COSO expected no change to the assertions.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the framework changed. But the COSO edition has no bearing on whether 404(b) applies; COSO expects the assertions to stay as they were.

tips: Eliminate: B and C. Item 308(a) looks only at the latest year-end, and the COSO edition has no bearing on whether 404(b) applies.
Final two: D beats A because COSO expects no change to the 404 assertions; principle-by-principle work supports one overall ICFR conclusion.
Exam cue: COSO 2013 changed how management supports its assessment, not what Section 404 asks it to say.

questions.subtopic: 5A1 The original framework (1992). Before the principles
questions.question: A controller on the SOX team, trained on COSO's 1992 framework, asks how the 2013 update's 17 principles relate to it. According to COSO's 2013 FAQ, which statement is MOST accurate?

options.A: The 1992 text lacked these ideas; the 17 principles were wholly new
options.B: The principles formalize concepts already in the 1992 framework
options.C: The 1992 framework listed the same 17 principles under other names
options.D: The principles were borrowed from COSO's 2004 ERM framework

questions.pre_read: Ask whether the ideas behind the principles existed in 1992, and in what form.
questions.correct_explanation: COSO's 2013 FAQ explains that a significant change in the update was formalizing fundamental concepts introduced in the original 1992 framework; in the update, those concepts became principles. So the ideas were already present in 1992, embedded in the text rather than set out as a numbered list. Formalizing them was meant to clarify what effective internal control requires.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the numbered list first appeared in 2013. But COSO says the principles formalize concepts the original framework had already introduced.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: the ideas were there in 1992, but embedded in the text; the 1992 framework did not list them as 17 named principles.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because ERM is also a COSO framework. But COSO says the principles formalize concepts from the original internal control framework itself.

tips: Eliminate: A and D. COSO says the 2013 principles formalize ideas from the original text, so they are neither brand new nor borrowed from ERM.
Final two: B beats C because the 1992 framework held these ideas inside its text; it did not list 17 named principles.

questions.subtopic: 5A2 The 2013 update. Cyber controls without a foundation
questions.question: An online broker's IT team runs strong firewalls, but the board sets no cyber priorities and nobody checks that controls keep working. According to COSO in the Cyber Age, which weakness is MOST fundamental?

options.A: Control environment and monitoring, on which cyber controls depend
options.B: Control activities, since more technical layers would close the gap
options.C: Risk assessment, since threats should be ranked before any firewall is chosen
options.D: Information and communication, since cyber attacks get reported too slowly

questions.key_concept: COSO in the Cyber Age treats the control environment and monitoring as foundational: without them, cyber control activities are unlikely to work.
questions.pre_read: Sort the facts into components: what the board does, what IT runs, and who checks that controls keep working.
questions.correct_explanation: COSO in the Cyber Age calls the control environment and monitoring activities foundational to managing cyber risk: unless they are present and functioning, an organization is unlikely to understand its cyber risks, deploy well-designed control activities or respond appropriately. Here the board sets no cyber priorities, a control environment gap, and nobody evaluates the controls, a monitoring gap. More technical layers would fix neither.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: layered technical controls matter, but the paper says they are unlikely to work without a functioning control environment and monitoring, which are missing here.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because risk assessment comes before control activities. But nothing shows threats went unranked; the facts show missing board priorities and missing evaluations, which the paper calls foundational.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because cyber events must be communicated. But nothing shows slow reporting; the gaps are the board's priorities and the evaluations of controls.

tips: Eliminate: C and D. The facts show no unranked threats and no reporting delay; they show missing priorities and missing evaluations.
Final two: A beats B because the paper says cyber controls are unlikely to work unless the control environment and monitoring are present and functioning.
Exam cue: no tone from the board and no one checking controls means the foundation is missing, whatever the technology.

questions.subtopic: 5B2 ERM (2017): strategy and performance. Results below plan
questions.question: After two years of results well below plan, a retailer's management examines whether its risk-taking caused the shortfall and its risk practices need changing. Under COSO's 2017 ERM framework, which component is this MOST directly?

options.A: Performance, which identifies and assesses risks to objectives
options.B: Strategy and objective-setting, which sets the risk appetite
options.C: Review and revision, which reviews risk and performance
options.D: Information, communication and reporting, which reports on risk

questions.key_concept: ERM 2017's review and revision component reviews entity performance, considers risk and revises enterprise risk management practices (principles 15 to 17).
questions.pre_read: Ask whether management is handling risks going forward or looking back at results to adjust its practices.
questions.correct_explanation: COSO's 2017 framework places Reviews Risk and Performance, principle 16, and Pursues Improvement in Enterprise Risk Management, principle 17, in the review and revision component: by reviewing entity performance, the organization considers how well its ERM components work and what revisions are needed. The performance component identifies, assesses and responds to risks; it does not look back at results to revise risk practices.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the performance component identifies, assesses and responds to risks; looking back at results to revise risk practices is principle 16, in review and revision.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because poor results may change strategy. But this component sets appetite and strategy; reviewing results and practices sits in review and revision.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because results get reported. But principle 20 reports on risk, culture and performance; it does not evaluate and revise the practices.

tips: Eliminate: B and D. Setting appetite and reporting results are not the same as looking back to judge and revise risk practices.
Final two: C beats A because the performance component works risks forward; reviewing entity performance and revising ERM is principle 16, in review and revision.

questions.subtopic: 5A2 The 2013 update. A smaller company's controls
questions.question: A small issuer with 60 employees has few written procedures, but its finance director reviews every payment and each monthly reconciliation. Under COSO 2013, which view of its internal control is MOST accurate?

options.A: It can be effective if components and principles are present and functioning
options.B: It cannot be effective without written procedures for every principle
options.C: It is effective by default, since COSO exempts smaller companies
options.D: It cannot be effective until the company adopts COSO's separate ERM framework

questions.key_concept: COSO 2013 allows a smaller entity's internal control to be less formal and structured yet effective, judged by the same present-and-functioning test.
questions.pre_read: Separate how formal a control system is from whether its components and principles work.
questions.correct_explanation: COSO's 2013 executive summary says the framework applies to entities of every size, and that a smaller entity's system of internal control may be less formal and less structured yet still be effective. Effectiveness turns on each component and relevant principle being present and functioning and the components operating together, not on how much is written down. Size brings no exemption from that test.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: documentation helps show principles are present, and SEC rules require evidence for management's assessment, but COSO accepts a less formal system in a smaller entity.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because COSO recognizes smaller entities. But it grants no exemption; the same present-and-functioning test applies to every entity.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because ERM sounds more complete. But the internal control framework sets its own test for effectiveness; it does not depend on adopting ERM.

tips: Eliminate: C and D. COSO gives smaller entities no exemption and does not make ERM a condition of effective internal control.
Final two: A beats B because COSO accepts a less formal, less structured system in a smaller entity if components and principles are present and functioning.
Exam cue: in COSO, effectiveness depends on components and principles that work, not on the volume of paperwork.

options.B: Strategy setting came into COSO's work with the 2013 internal control update
options.C: Strategy belongs to the board alone, so neither ERM edition addresses it
options.D: The 2004 definition already applied ERM in strategy setting; 2017 expanded it

tips: Eliminate: B and C. The 2013 update was to internal control, and strategy appears in both ERM editions.

questions.subtopic: 5C1 Software and spreadsheets. IT frameworks such as COBIT

questions.subtopic: 5A1 The original framework (1992). How much assurance is reasonable
questions.question: A CFO asks how demanding 'reasonable assurance' is in the SEC's Section 404 rules. Under Release No. 33-8810, it means the degree of assurance that would satisfy:

options.A: prudent officials in the conduct of their own affairs
options.B: the audit committee, under the company's own risk appetite
options.C: the independent auditor, under the PCAOB's auditing standards
options.D: the SEC staff that its one prescribed method was followed

questions.key_concept: Under Release No. 33-8810, reasonable assurance is what would satisfy prudent officials, an objective test with no single required method.
questions.pre_read: Look for the standard the SEC borrows from the Exchange Act, and what it says reasonableness does not require.
questions.correct_explanation: Release No. 33-8810 explains that the reasonable assurance in the SEC's Section 404 rules relates to the FCPA's language: Exchange Act Section 13(b)(7) defines it as the degree of assurance that would satisfy prudent officials in the conduct of their own affairs. The SEC adds that this objective standard still allows a range of judgments, with no single conclusion or methodology.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the audit committee oversees financial reporting. But the release takes an objective test from Exchange Act Section 13(b)(7), not a level each committee sets.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the independent auditor attests under 404(b). But the term comes from Exchange Act Section 13(b)(7), applied by the SEC to management; auditing standards do not define it.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: the SEC does guide management's evaluation, but it says 'reasonable' in Section 404 implies no single conclusion or methodology.

tips: Eliminate: B and C. The release borrows an objective test from the Exchange Act; it does not let the audit committee or the independent auditor set the level.
Final two: A beats D because Release No. 33-8810 ties the term to what would satisfy prudent officials, allowing a range of judgments and no single method.
Exam cue: 'reasonable' in Section 404 is the prudent-official test from Exchange Act Section 13(b)(7): objective, yet open to a range of judgments and methods.

questions.subtopic: 5A1 The original framework (1992). Guidance and the framework
questions.question: Which response is MOST accurate under SEC Release No. 33-8810 when a SOX lead proposes dropping COSO 2013 because the release now explains how management evaluates ICFR?

options.A: Drop it; the release itself now serves as the control framework
options.B: Drop it once the independent auditor agrees to the new approach
options.C: Keep it for entity-level controls; use the release for the rest
options.D: Keep a framework; the release does not replace its control elements

questions.key_concept: The SEC's 2007 interpretive guidance explains how to evaluate ICFR; it does not replace the control framework management uses.
questions.pre_read: Recall what the SEC's 2007 release says about its own role.
questions.correct_explanation: Release No. 33-8810 is interpretive guidance describing one way for management to evaluate ICFR. It says the evaluation covers the entity-wide and pervasive elements of internal control defined by management's selected framework, and that the guidance is not intended to replace the elements of an effective system of internal control that a framework defines. Management keeps a framework and uses the release to guide its evaluation.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the release does guide the evaluation, but it says it is not meant to replace the control elements that a framework defines.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the independent auditor attests under 404(b). But the auditor's agreement cannot turn guidance into a framework; the choice is management's.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because entity-level controls come from the framework. But the framework defines the elements of internal control throughout; the release replaces none of them.

tips: Eliminate: B and C. The independent auditor cannot swap guidance for a framework, and the release replaces no part of one.
Final two: D beats A because Release No. 33-8810 says it does not replace the elements of internal control defined in a framework.
Exam cue: the framework defines effective internal control; the SEC's 2007 guidance describes how management can evaluate against it.

questions.subtopic: 5A1 The original framework (1992). Self-assessment
questions.question: Under SEC Release No. 33-8810, for management's ICFR evaluation, evidence from self-assessments by the people who operate a control generally:

options.A: carries the same weight as direct testing by internal audit
options.B: replaces direct testing, even where ICFR risk is high
options.C: gives less evidence, as its preparers are less objective
options.D: cannot count as evidence in management's ICFR evaluation

questions.key_concept: Release No. 33-8810 accepts self-assessments as ongoing monitoring evidence but gives less weight to those by a control's own operators.
questions.pre_read: Think about who performs the self-assessment and how close they are to the control.
questions.correct_explanation: Release No. 33-8810 counts self-assessment among ongoing monitoring activities and notes it covers procedures by people with varying degrees of objectivity. Self-assessments by the people who operate the control generally provide less evidence, because their objectivity is lower. As ICFR risk rises, management uses more objective people or direct testing; where risk is high, evidence ordinarily comes from direct testing or monitoring by more objective individuals.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because both are evaluations. But the release ties the weight of evidence to objectivity, and the people who run a control are the least objective about it.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because self-assessment is cheap and frequent. But where ICFR risk is high the release looks for direct testing or monitoring by more objective people.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: the release does discount these self-assessments, but it still counts them as ongoing monitoring evidence; they weigh less, they are not excluded.

tips: Eliminate: A and B. The release weighs evidence by objectivity, and high-risk areas call for direct testing or more objective monitors.
Final two: C beats D because the SEC counts self-assessment as monitoring evidence; it gives less weight, not none.
Exam cue: the further the checker is from running a control, the more the evidence weighs.

questions.subtopic: 5A2 The 2013 update. Deficiencies across components
questions.question: A nonprofit hospital's management, applying COSO 2013, finds each component present and functioning, with minor deficiencies spread across three components. Under COSO's FAQ, what MOST decides whether the components operate together?

options.A: Whether any single deficiency, judged alone, is a major deficiency
options.B: Whether all the deficiencies combined amount to a major deficiency
options.C: Whether each component is present and functioning, and nothing more
options.D: Whether every deficiency has been remediated before year-end

questions.key_concept: Components operate together when they are present and functioning and deficiencies aggregated across components are not a major deficiency.
questions.pre_read: Recall the two conditions COSO's FAQ sets for showing that the components operate together.
questions.correct_explanation: COSO 2013 requires each component and relevant principle to be present and functioning and the five components to operate together. COSO's FAQ says management can show they operate together when the components are present and functioning and the deficiencies, aggregated across components, do not amount to a major deficiency. Minor deficiencies in several components can combine into a major one, so they are judged together.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: each deficiency is judged for severity, but operating together also needs the deficiencies aggregated across components, since several minor ones can combine.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because presence and functioning come first. But COSO adds a separate requirement that the components operate together, judged on the deficiencies combined.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because fixing deficiencies helps. But COSO does not demand zero deficiencies; the test is whether those that remain amount, together, to a major deficiency.

tips: Eliminate: C and D. Operating together is a separate requirement, and COSO accepts remaining minor deficiencies that are not major in combination.
Final two: B beats A because COSO's FAQ judges operating together on deficiencies aggregated across components, not one at a time.
Exam cue: present, functioning and operating together; for the last, add up deficiencies across components before deciding.

questions.subtopic: 5A2 The 2013 update. A quarterly internal audit review
questions.question: Each quarter, a retailer's internal audit team visits accounts payable to check whether its controls are working. Under COSO 2013, this review is BEST classified as:

options.A: a separate evaluation, within the monitoring activities component
options.B: an ongoing evaluation, built into the accounts payable process itself
options.C: a control activity, since it examines individual payable transactions
options.D: a risk assessment, since it looks for weaknesses in the controls

questions.key_concept: Under COSO 2013, periodic evaluations performed apart from daily operations are separate evaluations within monitoring activities.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether the review runs inside the process every day or is performed periodically from outside it.
questions.correct_explanation: COSO 2013's monitoring activities use ongoing evaluations, separate evaluations or both to check that each component is present and functioning (principle 16). Ongoing evaluations are built into business processes and give timely information; separate evaluations are performed periodically, with scope and frequency set by risk and by how well ongoing evaluations work. A quarterly internal audit review apart from daily processing is a separate evaluation.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: both are monitoring, but ongoing evaluations run within the business process; a periodic internal audit review performed apart from daily work is separate.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the review looks at transactions. But control activities are the controls themselves; checking whether they work is monitoring.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the review finds weaknesses. But risk assessment analyzes risks to objectives; evaluating whether controls work belongs to monitoring.

tips: Eliminate: C and D. Checking whether controls work is monitoring, not a control itself or the analysis of risks to objectives.
Final two: A beats B because the review is periodic and outside daily processing; ongoing evaluations are built into the process.
Exam cue: built into the process and continuous means ongoing; periodic and apart from operations means separate.

questions.subtopic: 5A2 The 2013 update. A finding held until December
questions.question: A distributor's internal auditors find in March that a reconciliation is not performed, but company practice holds every audit finding until the board's December meeting. Under COSO 2013, which principle is MOST clearly not met?

options.A: Principle 16, on performing ongoing and separate evaluations
options.B: Principle 5, on holding individuals accountable for controls
options.C: Principle 10, on selecting control activities that reduce risk
options.D: Principle 17, on communicating deficiencies in a timely manner

questions.key_concept: COSO's principle 17 requires deficiencies to be evaluated and communicated in time to those responsible for corrective action.
questions.pre_read: Separate what the internal auditors did from what happened to their finding afterwards.
questions.correct_explanation: Principle 17, under monitoring activities, has the organization evaluate internal control deficiencies and communicate them in a timely manner to those responsible for corrective action, including senior management and the board as appropriate. The internal auditors did evaluate the controls and found the deficiency, so the evaluation step worked; holding the finding for nine months fails the timely-communication principle.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: principle 16 covers the evaluations themselves, and the auditors performed one and found the deficiency; the delay is in communicating it.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because reported findings lead to accountability. But principle 5 is about holding people responsible for their duties, not when deficiencies are reported.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because a fix may need new controls. But principle 10 covers selecting control activities, not reporting deficiencies to those who must act.

tips: Eliminate: B and C. Accountability and the selection of control activities do not govern when deficiencies reach those who must act.
Final two: D beats A because the evaluation happened and found the deficiency; principle 17 requires reporting it in time for corrective action.
Exam cue: found but not reported in time points to principle 17; never evaluated points to principle 16.

questions.subtopic: 5A2 The 2013 update. Who is accountable
questions.question: A new director asks where responsibility for the company's system of internal control rests. In COSO 2013's executive summary, the party MOST directly accountable for internal control is:

options.A: the board of directors, which oversees internal control
options.B: the internal auditors, who review how controls are applied
options.C: senior management, which in turn answers to the board
options.D: the independent auditor, which examines ICFR from outside

questions.key_concept: COSO 2013 makes senior management accountable for internal control and to the board, which oversees and challenges management.
questions.pre_read: Recall how COSO's summary describes each party's part in internal control.
questions.correct_explanation: COSO's executive summary, describing how each party uses the framework, says senior management is accountable for internal control and to the board of directors. The board discusses the state of internal control with senior management, oversees it and challenges management where needed, seeking input from internal and external auditors. Auditors evaluate internal control; they are not accountable for running it.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the board oversees internal control, but COSO makes senior management accountable for it and to the board; oversight is not accountability.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because internal auditors evaluate controls. But they review and report; COSO places accountability for the system with senior management.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the auditor reports on ICFR. But the independent auditor examines the system for its own report; it is not accountable for running it.

tips: Eliminate: B and D. Internal and independent auditors evaluate controls; neither is accountable for the company's system of internal control.
Final two: C beats A because COSO says senior management is accountable for internal control and to the board, which oversees and challenges.
Exam cue: in COSO's internal control framework, senior management is accountable and the board oversees; auditors evaluate.

questions.subtopic: 5A2 The 2013 update. Duties that cannot be split
questions.question: At a 12-person subsidiary, one accountant both records cash receipts and reconciles the bank account, and management cannot add staff. Under COSO 2013, which response BEST fits the framework?

options.A: Use alternative controls, such as a manager reviewing each reconciliation
options.B: Accept the risk, since COSO excuses smaller units from segregating duties
options.C: Report a material weakness, since COSO bars combining these duties
options.D: Move the monthly reconciliation to the independent auditor's team

questions.key_concept: Where segregation of duties is not practical, COSO 2013 expects management to select and develop alternative control activities.
questions.pre_read: Ask what COSO says management does when the usual control, split duties, cannot be applied.
questions.correct_explanation: COSO 2013 says segregation of duties is typically built into the selection and development of control activities, and that where it is not practical, management selects and develops alternative control activities. A manager's review of each bank reconciliation addresses the risk that one person could both take cash and hide it. Leaving the risk unaddressed is not COSO's answer, and the reconciliation stays the company's own control.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: accepting a risk can be a valid choice elsewhere, but where duties cannot be split COSO expects management to select alternative control activities.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because combined duties are a classic finding. But COSO does not bar them; where segregation is not practical it asks management for alternative control activities.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the auditor is independent. But the reconciliation is the company's own control; an independent auditor performing it would be doing management's work.

tips: Eliminate: C and D. COSO does not treat combined duties as an automatic failure where segregation is impractical, and the independent auditor cannot run the company's controls.
Final two: A beats B because COSO answers impractical segregation with alternative control activities, not by leaving the risk unaddressed.
Exam cue: duties cannot be split? Look for the compensating review or other alternative control, not an exemption.

questions.subtopic: 5A2 The 2013 update. A season the weather ruined
questions.question: After an almost snowless winter, a ski resort misses its revenue goals; management could neither predict nor soften the weather. Under COSO 2013, what does effective internal control MOST accurately give the board?

options.A: Reasonable assurance that its revenue goals are met despite the weather
options.B: Absolute assurance that weather losses stay within the board's budget
options.C: No assurance, because COSO leaves operations objectives to ERM
options.D: Reasonable assurance it understands how well operations are managed

questions.key_concept: For external events that may significantly affect operations, effective internal control assures understanding of how operations are managed, not their achievement.
questions.pre_read: Notice whether the event could be predicted or mitigated, and what COSO promises for operations in that case.
questions.correct_explanation: COSO 2013 says that when external events may significantly affect operations objectives, effective internal control gives senior management and the board reasonable assurance that they understand the extent to which operations are managed effectively and efficiently. It cannot make goals happen despite such events; external events beyond the organization's control are among the framework's named limitations.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: COSO offers that when external events are unlikely to matter or can be predicted and mitigated; here they could be neither.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because budgets set limits. But a budget cannot stop the weather, and nothing in COSO promises that losses will stay within one.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because ERM is the broader framework. But operations is one of the internal control framework's own three objective categories.

tips: Eliminate: B and C. No framework can hold weather losses to a budget, and operations objectives belong to the internal control framework itself.
Final two: D beats A because, for events the resort could neither predict nor mitigate, COSO promises understanding of how operations are managed, not results.
Exam cue: for uncontrollable outside events, effective internal control means knowing where operations stand, not guaranteed results.

questions.subtopic: 5B2 ERM (2017): strategy and performance. Plants assessed one by one
questions.question: At a food maker, each plant manager assesses risks within their own plant, though contamination at one plant would force recalls across every brand. Under COSO's 2017 ERM executive summary, what is MOST clearly missing?

options.A: A finer rating scale for the risks at each plant
options.B: A yearly internal audit of each plant's food safety controls
options.C: Managing risks entity-wide, as one part's risk can hit another
options.D: One combined register listing every plant's risks in one place

questions.key_concept: COSO's 2017 summary lists managing risk entity-wide as an ERM benefit, since a risk can start in one part of an entity and affect another.
questions.pre_read: Notice where the risk starts and where its effects would land.
questions.correct_explanation: Among the benefits of ERM, COSO's 2017 executive summary lists identifying and managing risk entity-wide: a risk can originate in one part of the entity but affect a different part, so management identifies and manages these entity-wide risks to sustain and improve performance. Plant-by-plant assessments miss exactly the contamination risk that spreads across brands.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because ratings can be refined. But a finer scale still rates each plant alone; the gap is a risk that crosses plants.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because audits test controls. But a yearly audit of each plant still looks plant by plant; it does not manage a risk that spreads across the entity.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: a combined register gathers the risks, but listing them side by side does not manage how a risk in one plant affects the others.

tips: Eliminate: A and B. A finer scale and a plant-level audit both still look at one plant at a time.
Final two: C beats D because listing every plant's risks together does not manage how one plant's risk hits the others; COSO names entity-wide management as the benefit.
Exam cue: when a risk starts in one unit but lands in another, look for the entity-wide answer, not a better list or a local fix.

questions.subtopic: 5B2 ERM (2017): strategy and performance. Ranking assessed risks
questions.question: A bank's risk team has identified and assessed its risks and must now rank them. Under COSO's 2017 ERM framework, which basis for ranking is MOST accurate?

options.A: Likelihood alone, so the most probable risks come first
options.B: Severity, in the context of the bank's risk appetite
options.C: The order in which the business lines report them
options.D: Severity, measured against each business line's own budget

questions.key_concept: In COSO's 2017 framework, assessed risks are prioritized by severity in the context of risk appetite.
questions.pre_read: Recall what yardstick the 2017 summary uses once risks have been assessed.
questions.correct_explanation: COSO's 2017 executive summary describes the performance component: risks that may affect strategy and business objectives are identified and assessed, then prioritized by severity in the context of risk appetite, before the organization selects risk responses. Appetite, set with strategy, is the yardstick for the ranking.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because likely risks feel urgent. But the framework ranks risks by severity in the context of risk appetite, not by probability alone.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because business lines raise risks first. But reporting order is not a ranking; the framework prioritizes by severity against appetite.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: severity is the right measure, but the framework reads it in the context of the entity's risk appetite, not each business line's budget.

tips: Eliminate: A and C. Probability alone and reporting order are not the framework's basis for ranking.
Final two: B beats D because COSO prioritizes risks by severity in the context of risk appetite, not against local budgets.
Exam cue: in ERM 2017, rank by severity and read it against risk appetite.

questions.subtopic: 5B2 ERM (2017): strategy and performance. Effective ICFR and ERM
questions.question: A director argues that because the company's Section 404 reports show effective ICFR, it already has enterprise risk management. Under COSO's 2017 ERM executive summary, which response is MOST accurate?

options.A: Agreed; for an SEC filer, effective ICFR amounts to ERM
options.B: Agreed, once the independent auditor's 404(b) opinion is clean
options.C: Not yet; ERM just adds a longer list of non-financial risks
options.D: Not yet; ERM also covers strategy, governance and performance

questions.key_concept: COSO's 2017 summary says ERM addresses more than internal control, so effective ICFR does not show ERM is in place.
questions.pre_read: Compare what a Section 404 report covers with what COSO's 2017 summary says ERM covers.
questions.correct_explanation: COSO's 2017 executive summary, clearing up misconceptions, says enterprise risk management addresses more than internal control: it also addresses strategy-setting, governance, communicating with stakeholders and measuring performance, and its principles apply at all levels and across all functions. Effective ICFR shows that one part of internal control works; it does not show that ERM is in place.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because Section 404 is the SEC's control requirement. But ICFR covers reliable financial reporting; COSO says ERM reaches well beyond internal control.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the independent auditor's opinion adds assurance. But a 404(b) opinion is about ICFR too; it says nothing about strategy-setting or governance of risk.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: ERM does look beyond financial risks, but COSO says it addresses strategy-setting, governance, stakeholder communication and performance, not just more risks.

tips: Eliminate: A and B. Effective ICFR, with or without a clean 404(b) opinion, is about financial reporting controls, not the whole of ERM.
Final two: D beats C because COSO says ERM addresses more than internal control, including strategy-setting, governance and performance, not just more risks.
Exam cue: effective ICFR answers Section 404; it does not show that ERM is in place.

questions.subtopic: 5B2 ERM (2017): strategy and performance. A principles checklist
questions.question: A chief risk officer plans to show the board that ERM is in place by ticking off each principle of COSO's 2017 framework once a year. Under the framework's executive summary, which response is BEST?

options.B: The checklist works if internal audit signs off each line
options.C: The checklist should use the internal control principles instead
options.D: The checklist works if the board signs it off every year

questions.key_concept: COSO's 2017 summary says ERM is not a checklist but principles on which processes are built, and a system of monitoring, learning and improving.
questions.pre_read: Think about whether ticking principles shows how risk shapes decisions.
questions.correct_explanation: COSO's 2017 executive summary, clearing up misconceptions, says ERM is not a checklist: it is a set of principles on which processes can be built or integrated for a particular organization, and a system of monitoring, learning and improving performance. A yearly tick-box shows that principles were listed, not that they shape how the organization sets strategy and manages performance.

wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: board oversight matters to ERM, but a yearly sign-off on ticked principles is still a checklist; the summary describes principles to build processes on.

tips: Eliminate: B and C. An internal audit sign-off or a different list of principles keeps the tick-box approach.
Final two: A beats D because the summary says ERM is not a checklist at all; board approval does not change that.

questions.subtopic: 5B2 ERM (2017): strategy and performance. Results far above plan
questions.question: A furniture maker's plant produced 30% more than planned, and the risk officer flags the result to the board as a concern. Under COSO's 2017 ERM executive summary, which view is MOST accurate?

options.A: The surplus shows internal control over reporting has failed
options.B: The surplus automatically breaches the board's risk appetite
options.C: A big overshoot can be as troubling as a shortfall
options.D: The flag is wrong; strong output calls for a wider strategy

questions.key_concept: ERM 2017 lists reducing performance variability as a benefit: results far above plan can concern as much as shortfalls.
questions.pre_read: Recall the benefits COSO's 2017 summary lists, and whether they look only at shortfalls.
questions.correct_explanation: Among the benefits of ERM, COSO's 2017 executive summary lists reducing performance variability: for some entities the challenge is less surprises and losses than variability, and performing ahead of schedule or beyond expectations may cause as much concern as falling short. ERM helps anticipate the risks that affect performance and act to minimize disruption and maximize opportunity.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because surprises can point to control gaps. But higher output shows variability in operations, not a failure of internal control over financial reporting.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: appetite does matter to performance, but beating a plan does not by itself breach appetite; COSO's point is that large swings either way disrupt.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because strong results invite growth. But COSO's summary treats performance well beyond plan as a concern to manage, not proof the strategy should widen.

tips: Eliminate: A and D. Extra output is not a reporting control failure, and COSO does not treat a large surplus as proof to expand.
Final two: C beats B because COSO's summary names performance variability, up or down, as a concern; exceeding plan does not breach appetite by itself.
Exam cue: in ERM 2017, a big miss above plan can be a risk signal too; variability either way matters.

questions.subtopic: 5B2 ERM (2017): strategy and performance. What counts as risk
questions.question: A risk officer compares how COSO's 2013 internal control framework and its 2017 ERM framework define risk. Which difference is MOST accurate?

options.A: Internal control counts good and bad effects; ERM 2017 counts harm
options.B: ERM 2017 covers effects on strategy and objectives, good or bad
options.C: ERM 2017 limits risk to threats to reliable financial reporting
options.D: Both define risk alike, as an event that causes a loss

questions.key_concept: Internal control defines risk as an adverse effect on objectives; ERM 2017 covers any effect on strategy and business objectives.
questions.pre_read: Compare the verb each framework uses for how an event affects objectives.
questions.correct_explanation: COSO's internal control framework defines risk as the possibility that an event will occur and adversely affect the achievement of objectives. The 2017 ERM framework, as COSO's 2020 compliance paper quotes it, defines risk as the possibility that events will occur and affect the achievement of strategy and business objectives, and its summary stresses considering both positive and negative aspects of risk.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: it names the right contrast but reverses it; the internal control definition is adverse, while ERM 2017 also weighs positive aspects.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because SOX centers on financial reporting. But ERM 2017 ties risk to strategy and business objectives across the entity, not to one report.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because many people equate risk with loss. But the two definitions differ; ERM 2017's covers effects on strategy and objectives either way.

tips: Eliminate: C and D. ERM 2017 reaches strategy and all business objectives, and the two definitions are worded differently.
Final two: B beats A because the adverse-only wording belongs to internal control; ERM 2017 also weighs positive aspects.
Exam cue: internal control risk is adverse to objectives; ERM 2017 risk is any effect on strategy and objectives, upside included.
