questions.subtopic: 5A1 The original framework (1992). Evidence from daily interaction
questions.question: Under SEC Release No. 33-8810, which view is MOST accurate when an issuer with four operating segments and several reporting layers supports its ICFR conclusion mainly with the CFO's daily interaction with controls?

options.A: Enough, provided the CFO documents the interaction monthly
options.B: Not enough; the SEC rejects daily interaction as evidence
options.C: Enough once the independent auditor retests the controls
options.D: Not enough here; add direct testing or ongoing monitoring

questions.key_concept: Under Release No. 33-8810, daily interaction can support the evaluation in small, centralized companies, but generally not where there are several reporting layers or segments.
questions.pre_read: Notice how the company is organized before judging what evidence the CFO's involvement can give.
questions.correct_explanation: Release No. 33-8810 says daily interaction may give management enough knowledge to evaluate controls in smaller companies, for example where controls are centralized and few people are involved. With multiple reporting layers or operating segments it generally would not, because those assessing ICFR would not ordinarily know the controls' operation well enough; management would ordinarily use direct testing or ongoing monitoring-type procedures.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: documenting the basis matters, but records do not cure the problem here: across segments and layers the CFO cannot know enough about how the controls operate.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because direct testing is common. But the release accepts daily interaction as evidence in smaller, centralized companies; it is the facts here that rule it out.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the independent auditor tests controls. But management needs its own evidence for its assessment; the auditor's tests support the auditor's report.

tips: Eliminate: B and C. The release does accept daily interaction in the right setting, and management's evidence cannot be the auditor's retesting.
Final two: D beats A because with several segments and reporting layers daily interaction generally is not sufficient, however well it is documented.
Exam cue: daily interaction can carry a small, centralized company; layers and segments call for direct testing or monitoring.

questions.subtopic: 5A1 The original framework (1992). No fraud found so far
questions.question: Under SEC Release No. 33-8810, which response is MOST accurate when a smaller issuer's CFO proposes leaving fraud out of this year's ICFR risk assessment because no fraud has ever been found?

options.A: Assess it; fraud risk exists even where none has been found
options.B: Agreed; fraud risk is assessed once a fraud has been found
options.C: Leave it to the independent auditor, who assesses fraud risk
options.D: Agreed; a smaller company may skip fraud risk at its size

questions.key_concept: Under Release No. 33-8810, management assesses fraud risk every year; it exists in any organization, and size scales the work rather than removing it.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the SEC says about fraud risk in companies of different sizes.
questions.correct_explanation: Release No. 33-8810 says management's evaluation of misstatement risk should consider the entity's vulnerability to fraud, such as fraudulent financial reporting, misappropriation of assets and corruption. The risk of material misstatement due to fraud ordinarily exists in any organization, regardless of size or type, and the absence of an identified fraud does not show that no fraud risk exists. Size changes how much work is needed.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because a found fraud demands attention. But the release treats fraud risk as part of every year's risk assessment; waiting for a fraud reverses the logic.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the independent auditor considers fraud in its audit. But management's own risk assessment must cover fraud; the auditor's work does not stand in for it.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: the release does scale fraud-risk work to size and complexity, but it says fraud risk ordinarily exists in any organization, so it cannot be skipped.

tips: Eliminate: B and C. Fraud risk is assessed before any fraud is found, and management cannot hand its risk assessment to the independent auditor.
Final two: A beats D because size changes how much fraud-risk work is done, not whether it is done.
Exam cue: no fraud found is never evidence of no fraud risk.

questions.subtopic: 5C1 Software and spreadsheets. A payment block in the ERP
questions.question: Management configures its ERP system to reject automatically any payment to a bank account missing from the approved vendor master file. Under COSO 2013, this control is MOST accurately described as:

options.A: a detective control activity, performed automatically after payment
options.B: a preventive control activity, performed automatically by the system
options.C: a general control over technology, since it runs inside the ERP
options.D: a monitoring activity, since it evaluates whether controls work

questions.key_concept: COSO 2013 control activities may be preventive or detective and manual or automated; a system rule that blocks a payment is preventive.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether the control stops the payment before it happens or finds it afterwards.
questions.correct_explanation: COSO 2013 describes control activities as actions set through policies and procedures that may be preventive or detective and may be manual or automated, performed at all levels and over the technology environment. A system rule that stops an unauthorized payment before it is made is a preventive, automated control activity. A check after payment would be detective.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the control is automated, but detective controls find problems after they occur; this rule stops the payment before it is made.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the rule runs in the ERP. But general controls over technology protect the IT environment itself; this rule screens individual payments.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the rule checks payments. But monitoring evaluates whether components and controls work; this rule is itself the control.

tips: Eliminate: C and D. General controls protect the IT environment and monitoring evaluates controls; this rule screens each payment itself.
Final two: B beats A because the rule stops the payment before it happens, which is preventive; detective controls find errors afterwards.
Exam cue: stops it beforehand means preventive, finds it afterwards means detective; manual or automated is a separate question.

questions.subtopic: 5C1 Software and spreadsheets. A spreadsheet fed by outside data
questions.question: A treasury team values derivatives in a spreadsheet fed by a vendor's price file; its reviewer checks formulas but never whether that external data is reliable. Under COSO 2013, which principle is MOST at risk?

options.A: Principle 11, on general control activities over technology
options.B: Principle 14, on communicating information internally
options.C: Principle 13, on using relevant, quality information
options.D: Principle 16, on ongoing and separate evaluations

questions.key_concept: COSO's principle 13 requires relevant, quality information; correct formulas applied to unchecked external data still leave the control weak.
questions.pre_read: Note what the reviewer checks and what goes unchecked before matching a principle.
questions.correct_explanation: Principle 13, under information and communication, has the organization obtain or generate and use relevant, quality information, from internal and external sources, to support internal control. The vendor file is external data feeding a valuation; checking formulas but not the data leaves the information's quality untested. COSO's FAQ notes that quality information supports control activities, so a weak feed undermines the review itself.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the spreadsheet is technology, but its formulas are being checked; the gap is the quality of the outside data feeding it.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because information is involved. But principle 14 covers communicating information inside the organization, not whether incoming data is complete and current.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because a review is happening. But principle 16 covers evaluations of whether components work; the gap is the data the control relies on.

tips: Eliminate: B and D. Internal communication and evaluations of components do not address the quality of data the valuation uses.
Final two: C beats A because the formulas are reviewed; what goes untested is the external data, which principle 13 covers.
Exam cue: good formulas on bad data still give bad numbers; data quality points to principle 13.

questions.subtopic: 5C1 Software and spreadsheets. A spreadsheet policy no one carries out
questions.question: Management has decided that every key spreadsheet must be locked and reviewed, but it never assigns who does this, when or how, so nothing is done. Under COSO 2013, which principle is MOST clearly unmet?

options.A: Principle 4, on attracting, developing and keeping competent people
options.B: Principle 15, on communicating with external parties about controls
options.C: Principle 10, on selecting control activities that reduce risk
options.D: Principle 12, on deploying controls through policies and procedures

questions.key_concept: COSO's principle 12 deploys control activities through policies that set expectations and procedures that put them into action.
questions.pre_read: Notice what management decided and what it left unassigned.
questions.correct_explanation: Principle 12, under control activities, has the organization deploy control activities through policies that establish what is expected and procedures that put those policies into action. Here the policy sets the expectation, but with no one assigned and no timing or method, it never operates. The control was chosen; the gap is the procedure that turns the policy into practice.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because people carry out controls. But nothing suggests a lack of skill; the gap is that no procedure assigns the work.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because policies can be shared outside. But principle 15 covers external communication, not turning an internal policy into practice.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: principle 10 covers choosing controls, and the policy did choose locking and review; what is missing is the procedure that puts it into action.

tips: Eliminate: A and B. Nothing points to a skills gap or to communication with outside parties; the policy has no procedure behind it.
Final two: D beats C because the control was chosen; principle 12 requires procedures that put the policy into action.
Exam cue: a policy with no one assigned to carry it out points to principle 12: policies set the expectation, procedures make it happen.

questions.subtopic: 5C2 Service organizations: from SAS 70 to SSAE 18. Who a SOC 1 report is for
questions.question: A payroll processor's sales team wants to post its SOC 1 Type 2 report on its public website for prospects. According to the AICPA, SOC 1 reports are MOST specifically intended for:

options.A: the general public, as a freely distributed general-use report
options.B: the service organization's own investors and lenders
options.C: user entities and the auditors of their financial statements
options.D: the SEC staff, as an exhibit to each user's annual report

questions.key_concept: The AICPA aims SOC 1 reports at user entities and their auditors; the freely distributable general-use report is SOC 3.
questions.pre_read: Think about who needs a SOC 1 report's detail, and so who it is written for.
questions.correct_explanation: The AICPA says SOC 1 reports are specifically intended to meet the needs of the entities that use a service organization and of the CPAs who audit those user entities' financial statements, in evaluating the effect of the service organization's controls on the statements. The report meant for free distribution is a SOC 3, a general-use report on trust services criteria with less detail.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: that describes a SOC 3 report, which the AICPA treats as general use and freely distributable; a SOC 1 report is meant for user entities and their auditors.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because investors read reports. But a SOC 1 report covers controls over services to customers, not the processor's own financial statements.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because user companies file with the SEC. But the AICPA describes SOC 1 reports as meant for user entities and their auditors, not as a filing for SEC staff.

tips: Eliminate: B and D. SOC 1 covers controls over services to user entities, and it is not written for the SEC staff.
Final two: C beats A because a freely distributed, general-use report is a SOC 3; the AICPA aims SOC 1 at user entities and their auditors.
Exam cue: SOC 1 serves user entities and their auditors; SOC 3 is the general-use report that can be shared freely.

questions.subtopic: 5C2 Service organizations: from SAS 70 to SSAE 18. Which outsourced activity counts
questions.question: An issuer outsources four activities to outside providers. For management's Section 404 assessment, which provider's controls MOST clearly fall within the company's ICFR?

options.A: The cloud host that runs the company's public marketing web pages
options.B: The processor that pays suppliers and posts entries to the ledger
options.C: The consultant that designs the company's employee wellness program
options.D: The broker that places the company's property insurance cover

questions.key_concept: An outsourced activity matters for ICFR when it initiates, authorizes, records, processes or reports transactions in the financial statements.
questions.pre_read: Recall the kinds of outsourced activity the SEC staff's FAQ describes.
questions.correct_explanation: The SEC staff's ICFR FAQ describes outsourced activities that affect the initiation, authorization, recording, processing or reporting of transactions in the financial statements, giving payroll as its example. A processor that pays suppliers and posts the entries to the ledger processes and records transactions in the statements, so its controls matter for the assessment. A marketing website's host touches no financial transactions, even though it is an IT service.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: hosting is IT, and IT can be in scope, but this site carries marketing content and touches no transactions that reach the statements.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it is an outsourced service. But designing a wellness program does not initiate, record or process the company's financial transactions.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because insurance is a financial matter. But the broker only places the cover; the company itself records and pays the premiums.

tips: Eliminate: C and D. Neither provider initiates, records or processes the company's transactions; the company records those costs itself.
Final two: B beats A because the supplier-payment processor records transactions in the statements; a marketing website host does not, even though it is IT.
Exam cue: an outsourced activity counts for ICFR when it initiates, authorizes, records, processes or reports transactions in the statements.

questions.subtopic: 5C2 Service organizations: from SAS 70 to SSAE 18. A report that skips cyber controls
questions.question: An insurer's claims platform runs at a cloud provider whose service auditor report does not cover cyber controls. According to COSO in the Cyber Age, what should management MOST appropriately do?

options.A: Take steps to understand and monitor the provider's cyber controls
options.B: Rely on the report, since the provider answers for cyber controls
options.C: Ask the independent auditor to test the provider's cyber controls
options.D: Drop cyber risk from monitoring, since the platform is outsourced

questions.key_concept: When service auditor reports are missing or skip cyber controls, COSO in the Cyber Age says the user organization should understand those controls itself.
questions.pre_read: Recall what COSO in the Cyber Age says about cyber controls at outsourced providers.
questions.correct_explanation: COSO in the Cyber Age notes that many companies' IT environments extend to outsourced service providers, and lists monitoring of cyber risk and controls at those providers among the keys to effective monitoring. If service auditor reports are not provided or do not sufficiently address cyber controls, the user organization should take steps to understand those controls. Relying on a report that is silent on cyber controls leaves that risk unexamined.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: a service auditor's report is useful evidence, but this one omits cyber controls, and the paper says the user organization should then take its own steps.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the auditor tests controls. But monitoring is management's work; the independent auditor reports on its own engagement, not as management's monitor.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the provider runs the platform. But the paper lists monitoring outsourced providers' cyber risk and controls among the keys to effective monitoring.

tips: Eliminate: C and D. Monitoring belongs to management, and outsourcing does not take the provider's cyber risk out of it.
Final two: A beats B because the report does not cover cyber controls; the paper then expects the user organization to understand them itself.
Exam cue: a service auditor's report that skips a risk area leaves that area for the user company to understand and monitor.
